title: Ole Miss vs. Oklahoma postponed: New date, kickoff time announced
content:
College football teams faced an unexpected travel problem on Friday after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights across the country. Several teams struggled to reach their destinations, raising concerns about whether Saturday’s schedule would go ahead as planned.

The Colorado State Rams were among the affected teams. While waiting for clearance to fly to Pullman for their game against Washington State, the players held a walkthrough on the tarmac at Northern Colorado Regional Airport.

Now, Ole Miss also faced travel complications ahead of its Week 11 matchup against Oklahoma.

MORE: College football schedule facing major disruptions from FAA nationwide grounding

Ole Miss vs. Oklahoma rescheduled for Sunday

The SEC confirmed that the Rebels and Oklahoma will now meet on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET. The television network has yet to be determined.

Ole Miss was scheduled to leave Oxford on Friday ahead of its road game against Oklahoma, but they could not depart because of the FAA’s nationwide ground stoppage.

Even after the FAA lifted the restriction, they faced another problem. Its charter company could not accommodate a late-night departure, forcing the trip delayed to be delayed until Saturday afternoon.

GAME UPDATE:

The @OleMissFB at @OU_Football game has been moved to Sunday, Nov. 15 at 1 PM ET / Noon CT due to travel issues related to Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stoppage.

Television network is TBA.#SECFB pic.twitter.com/2B63eTmoTA

— Southeastern Conference (@SEC) November 14, 2026

Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny was far from pleased with the conference’s decision.

Oklahoma strongly objected to moving the game. The school immediately contacted Ole Miss and conference leadership after learning about the Rebels’ travel problems.

Denny acknowledged that the Rebels explored every possible option to reach Norman for Saturday’s game.

But he emphasized on the disruption it would cause Oklahoma fans who had already made travel arrangements, booked accommodation and organized their weekend around Saturday’s game.

“Put simply, this decision isn’t fair to our athletes, our institution, or to Sooner Nation,” Denny said.

He also disclosed that commissioner Greg Sankey informed Oklahoma that failing to play at the directed Sunday kickoff time would result in a forfeit.

The school also promised to share further information about game logistics and fan appreciation measures on Saturday.

title: MLB fans rip Jameson Taillon after ‘comically bad’ salary cap comment
content:
MLB‘s proposed changes to baseball’s financial system have sparked a heated debate among players and fans. Former Chicago Cubs pitcher Jameson Taillon strongly criticized the league’s proposal, calling it “comically bad.”

MLB shared its plan on X, outlining three major changes aimed at improving competitive balance and addressing local blackouts.

The proposal includes splitting all baseball-generated revenue equally between teams and players, introducing a salary cap and floor, and distributing media revenue equally among clubs.

MORE: Blue Jays’ Anthony Santander apologizes for sharing anti-Muslim videos

The league claimed the changes would reduce revenue differences and increase player compensation. It also argued that fans would get a more competitive product.

Baseball fans have repeatedly told us they have two issues with the game today: blackouts and fairness

We’re proposing to make three major changes to baseball:

1. Entering into a partnership with players where all revenues that are generated are split 50/50 between the teams… pic.twitter.com/GgeKshvFmN

— MLB (@MLB) November 13, 2026

Taillon, who recently became a free agent after finishing the 2026 season with Toronto, rejected that argument.

“This is comically bad,” Taillon wrote. “They’re being very careful and selective of what they’re saying/showing and how they’re delivering it.”

He accused MLB owners of using competitive balance as cover for reducing player salaries.

“At the end of the day- they want to drive down salaries and put more money in the pockets of billionaires,” he added.

This is comically bad. They’re being very careful and selective of what they’re saying/showing and how they’re delivering it. This is going to be ugly if they’re trying to sway fan/public support weeks before they even lock us out. At the end of the day- they want to drive down…

— Jameson Taillon (@JTaillon50) November 13, 2026

MLB fans challenge Jameson Taillon’s response

Taillon’s comments soon attracted reactions from baseball fans, with several questioning the players’ position.

One fan argued that supporters care more about competitive games, writing, “Fans don’t care about a fight about money between multi-millionaires and billionaires. Fans want competitiveness and to be able to watch the games without going bankrupt.”

Another pointed to Taillon’s previous earnings with the Cubs, writing, “You made $68 million as a Cub (over $2 mill per win). The MLB minimum salary is $1 mill.”

A fans supported the idea of a salary cap, arguing that smaller-market teams deserve a better chance to compete. He wrote, “Nah, fans of smaller market teams deserve to have hope like in the NFL. Markets like Green Bay, Buffalo, Kansas City, etc all have a chance in the NFL yearly. Us fans do want a salary cap system actually and more equal revenue sharing.”

However, some supporters criticized both sides, saying neither millionaires nor billionaires should present themselves as victims.

A fan wrote, “billionaires and multi-millionaires pretending they care about how much the journeyman backups make.”

billionaires and multi millionaires pretending they care about how much the journeyman backups make pic.twitter.com/CNh4eToCBp

— Rick “Socks” Owens (@ESPN_RickOwens) November 14, 2026

One fan said, “Lol keep pretending the players care any more about the fans than the owners do.”

A fan wrote, “Millionaire that makes 30 million a year is so relatable to us common folk!!!! Billionaire bad, hundred millionaires good!!! Durrrrr”

MORE: Pete Crow-Armstrong is only player in MLB history to accomplish these 5 feats in single season

The dispute comes with MLB’s collective bargaining agreement expiring on Dec. 1, 2026. Owners are pushing for a hard cap and floor, while the players’ union opposes a salary ceiling.

The disagreement could shape baseball’s next labor negotiations. For fans, the central question remains whether either side can deliver more competitive games and better access.

title: Red Sox To Sign Jake Bauers
content:
The Red Sox and first baseman Jake Bauers are in agreement on a four-year, $58MM contract, reports ESPN’s Jeff Passan. The VC Sports Group client received a $23.15MM qualifying offer from the Brewers but will turn that down and head to Boston on a lucrative multi-year contract.

Due in no small part to his postseason heroics, Bauers’ story is well known by now. The 31-year-old former top prospect was on the cusp of retirement after seemingly flaming out in the majors. He’d called his agent and informed him of the decision but changed course just days later when his wife learned she was pregnant with their second child and wouldn’t be going back to work — and securing health insurance — as they’d planned. Bauers signed back with the Brewers on a minor league deal ahead of the 2025 season and made the club. Bauers struggled for much of the season and looked like a DFA or non-tender candidate until a massive September saved his roster spot.

That September surge proved to be a portent for a full-fledged breakout. Bauers wasn’t just the Brewers’ best hitter and the eventual NLCS MVP in 2026 — he was one of the best hitters in the entire sport. Dating back to early September of 2025, Bauers has taken 631 regular season plate appearances and mashed at a .276/.396/.494 pace with 28 homers and a 16% walk rate. His 26.1% strikeout rate is too high, but for a player with this type of patience and power output, that’s a more than worthwhile trade-off.

By measure of wRC+, Bauers has been 48% better than average at the plate since September of 2025. Newly minted American League MVP Yordan Alvarez and Yankees star Ben Rice are the only two hitters with a better wRC+ than Bauers in that time. His 148 wRC+ places him in a four-way tie with Juan Soto, Shohei Ohtani and newly crowned NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong for the game’s third-best mark.

Bauers has averaged a whopping 92.1 mph off the bat with a huge 14% barrel rate and 51.9% hard-hit rate throughout his breakout, and his renaissance hasn’t been the product of selective matchups. While Bauers struggled against lefties for the majority of his career, he’s been platoon-proof throughout this turnaround, crushing lefties at a .267/.375/.526 pace with a 14.4% walk rate and 23% strikeout rate in 160 plate appearances.

Even if Bauers can’t sustain this level of nearly superhuman performance, there’s good reason to buy into him as a bona fide middle-of-the-order hitter now. In 2026, Statcast placed him in the top 10% of big league hitters in terms of average exit velocity, hard-hit rate, barrel rate, bat speed and expected wOBA. He was tied for the fourth-highest walk rate in baseball, and only 11 qualified hitters chased pitches off the plate at a lower rate than Bauers’ 21.7%.

Bauers had already hit his way into becoming a prominent piece of the Brewers’ lineup by the time the playoffs rolled around, but he thrust himself into the national spotlight with a monster NLCS performance against the Dodgers. Bauers flummoxed Yoshinobu Yamamoto with a marathon, 12-pitch at-bat that culminated in a walk, helping elevate the L.A. ace’s pitch count and chase him from the game in the third inning. He embarked on an 11-pitch battle against two-time Cy Young winning lefty Blake Snell the following night and did one better — belting a go-ahead two-run homer that played a pivotal role in Milwaukee’s sweep of the Dodgers. Bauers went 4-for-14 with that homer, a double and three walks en route to NLCS MVP honors.

The Red Sox are a surprising fit from a roster perspective, but they’re clearly prioritizing Bauers’ breakout production and sorting out the positional fit later. Willson Contreras played a fine first base in Boston last year, and the outfield — where Bauers is a stretch defensively anyhow — is already crowded. Ceddanne Rafaela is locked into center field, with Wilyer Abreu, Jarren Duran, Roman Anthony and Masataka Yoshida all in the mix for corner outfield/designated hitter time. Former first baseman Triston Casas, out since early 2025 with a major knee injury, is also still on the roster.

Boston is known to be shopping Duran, and Yoshida is a trade or release candidate himself as he enters the final season of a five-year deal that hasn’t gone to plan. Casas, like Duran, is a change of scenery candidate but also has minor league options remaining. If the Sox plan to move on from the Duran/Yoshida/Casas trio (or enter 2027 with Casas in the minors), they could go with Anthony, Rafaela and Abreu in the outfield, Contreras at first base, and Bauers as the primary designated hitter (with occasional reps at first base and in left field).

As MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker shows, Boston was projected for a bit more than $208MM prior to signing Bauers. We don’t know what next year’s luxury tax thresholds will be — or if the system will even be in place — but the Sox were already north of 2026’s $244MM CBT threshold. Bauers’ contract will add another $14.5MM annually to their tax considerations. The 2027 season would be their third consecutive year as tax payors, so they’d pay a 50% tax on the first $20MM by which they exceed the theoretical threshold, a 62% tax on the next $20MM, a 95% tax on the next $20MM and a 110% tax on anything beyond that point.

Because the Sox were tax payors for the 2026 season, they’ll have to forfeit their second- and fifth-highest draft selections in order to sign Bauers, who rejected his qualifying offer with the Brewers. Boston will also see next offseason’s bonus pool for signing international amateurs reduced by $1MM. The Brewers, meanwhile, will receive a compensatory pick for losing a free agent who’d been given a qualifying offer. Had Bauers signed for under $50MM, that pick would’ve come after Competitive Balance Round B — around No. 75 in the draft. Since he signed for more than $50MM, the pick will instead come at the end of the first round.

title: Giants Notes: Rotation, Bullpen, Catcher
content:
The Giants have made no secret of their desire to add at least one starter. They’re not planning to make a run at Tarik Skubal and seem to be out on Trevor Rogers, who’s attached to draft compensation via the qualifying offer. San Francisco has been loosely linked to Freddy Peralta and to NPB righty Kaima Taira, though there’s a decent chance they look more to the middle tiers of the market.

Logan Webb and Landen Roupp are the only two starters locked into the season-opening rotation. President of baseball operations Buster Posey has implicitly suggested that next season might be something of a bridge year with most of their top prospect talent in the lower minors. However, USA Today’s Bob Nightengale writes that they’re continuing to rebuff teams who call about Webb.

That’s not surprising, as the Giants publicly shot down speculation about trading their ace early in deadline season. Webb is signed for two more seasons. There’s a reasonable argument for listening on him if the Giants aren’t going to make an all-in push next year, but the organization clearly doesn’t want to embark on a full rebuild either. If they were going to listen on Webb, it’d have made more sense to do it over the summer when they were en route to a 97-loss season.

That leaves three spots up for grabs. Adrian Houser seems to have the leg up on one of those. Posey told Alex Pavlovic on the Giants Talk podcast that he “views Houser in the rotation,” though that came with a caveat the team was likely to deploy the opener more frequently. That’s not going to be unique to Houser, but he’ll be a frequent candidate as the team tries to navigate his deficiencies against left-handed hitters.

Houser’s sinker-heavy arsenal has been more effective against right-handed batters throughout his career. That was particularly true this year, as lefties teed off at a .282/.367/.516 clip with 12 homers in 284 plate appearances. Right-handed hitters mustered only a .222/.234/.318 mark across 186 trips. Houser would ideally be in a swing or pure relief role, but the Giants are paying him $13.5MM for the second season of his surprise $22MM contract. They also simply don’t have many alternatives in the starting staff with Hayden Birdsong, Blade Tidwell, Carson Whisenhunt and Trevor McDonald all set to miss part or all of the season recovering from Tommy John surgeries.

San Francisco is sure to bring in at least one starter and could leave an open competition among the likes of Anthony Molina, Matt Wilkinson, Yunior Marte and Cesar Perdomo for a spot. They’re also going to need to do a lot of work in the bullpen. That’s true at the back end, where Posey said they’re in the closing market. It also applies to the middle relief group — especially if they’re going to more aggressively play matchups to try to compensate for the lack of rotation depth.

Alex Pavlovic of NBC Sports Area and Shayna Rubin of The San Francisco Chronicle each wrote this week that the Giants are likely to bring in a left-handed reliever. They traded Erik Miller at the deadline and moved on from both Matt Gage and Reiver Sanmartin at season’s end. Sam Hentges is their only returning lefty reliever; he walked almost 15% of opponents in his first year back from shoulder surgery.

It’s a reasonably deep class of lefties on the free agent market. The Giants are highly unlikely to give up draft capital for Adrian Morejon and might be priced out on Alex Vesia and Gregory Soto. They could still look to old friend Steven Okert, Sean Newcomb, Brock Burke or A.J. Minter as borderline two-year deal candidates. José Alvarado and A.J. Puk are reclamation upside fliers, while Tim Hill and Hoby Milner are available as low-slot matchup specialists. Jon Heyman of The New York Post reported this week that the Giants were among the teams with interest in Hill, who led MLB with a 69% ground-ball rate for the Yankees this year.

While pitching is the front office’s focus, it’s possible they make a move behind the plate as well. Posey told Pavlovic on Giants Talk that bringing in a veteran catcher is “something we have to look at.” They traded Patrick Bailey in May and relied on three rookies — Daniel Susac, Drew Cavanaugh and Jesus Rodriguez — for a good chunk of the summer. Susac and Rodriguez each missed the final seven weeks of the season to injury, leading to Cavanaugh getting the bulk of the playing time down the stretch. They brought in journeyman Andrew Knizner as a stopgap backup but dropped him from the 40-man roster a couple weeks ago.

“We’re very excited about Susac, Cavanuagh and J-Rod, even (Adrián Sugastey) in Triple-A,” Posey told Pavlovic. “But they’re all young. It’s something we’ve talked about as a group. … It’s helpful for a young catcher to have a guy that’s done it for a while.” Veteran backup types available in free agency include Austin Hedges, James McCann, Christian Vázquez and Kyle Higashioka.

Rays Rumors: DeLuca, McClanahan, Pepiot, Rasmussen
content:
The Rays could make center fielder Jonny DeLuca available in trade this offseason, write Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic. The idea would be to open center field for Victor Mesa Jr., who played mostly right field this year.

DeLuca is coming off a career-best year in his third season as a Ray. He stole 17 bases and connected 11 home runs while batting .266/.300/.429 in a career-high 370 plate appearances. He divided his defensive workload between center and right field, playing strong defense at both spots. The 28-year-old missed a month with a right hamstring strain but was on the field much more often than he had been in 2025. The Oregon product was limited to 20 games that year by a right shoulder strain and a left hamstring injury.

The righty-hitting DeLuca provides most of his value in a speed and defense capacity. He’s a serviceable but unexceptional hitter, batting .250/.295/.389 in his career. DeLuca has had reverse platoon splits, posting a .709 OPS against righties compared to a .642 mark versus left-handed pitching. He has an aggressive approach and doesn’t make a ton of hard contact. He’s an elite runner who rates as one of the rangiest defensive outfielders in the game. DeLuca is under arbitration control for three seasons and projected by MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz for a $1.7MM salary.

Although Mesa isn’t quite as fast, he played very strong defense in a little over 500 right field innings. Mesa batted .260/.327/.498 with 14 home runs across 262 plate appearances, emerging as a key contributor after being acquired from Miami in a DFA trade. If the Rays were to play him more frequently in center field, they could look for a corner bat via free agency or trade. Ryan Vilade, Jacob Melton and Jack Suwinski are all on the 40-man roster. Top center field prospect Theo Gillen could open the season in Triple-A and might make his debut by the second half of 2027.

The Rays frequently deal role players as they get into their arbitration windows. There are a few similar possibilities on the pitching staff, as Rosenthal and Sammon suggest that starters Shane McClanahan and Ryan Pepiot could also be available. Although The Athletic report doesn’t mention Griffin Jax, one imagines the Rays will receive calls on him as well.

McClanahan and Jax are both entering their final arbitration years, respectively projected for $6.6MM and $5.7MM salaries. Pepiot is projected at $3.1MM and under club control for two seasons. All three pitchers are currently slated to be in Kevin Cash’s rotation, yet the Rays will surely be on the lookout for arms with more extended team control windows.

Pepiot, who was acquired alongside DeLuca in the 2023 Tyler Glasnow trade, missed all of 2026 recovering from right hip surgery. He pitched at a mid-rotation level before the injury, making 31 starts with a 3.67 ERA while striking out a quarter of opponents last year. President of baseball operations Erik Neander said last week that he’s expected to be full go for Spring Training.

McClanahan is a former ace who has struggled to stay healthy since undergoing elbow surgery three years ago. The 29-year-old southpaw remains effective when healthy, pitching to a 3.36 ERA with a league average strikeout and walk profile across 24 starts this past season. He had two injured list stints and missed the playoff run due to forearm tightness. He’s also expected to have a normal offseason.

Jax was the latest midseason bullpen to starter move for a Tampa Bay team that has had a lot of success in that regard. He worked 112 1/3 frames of 3.53 ERA ball and fanned a quarter of opposing hitters. He has plenty of experience at the back of the bullpen but looks like a capable mid-rotation starter. Tampa Bay will probably be in the rotation market even if they don’t move any of McClanahan, Jax or Pepiot. They’d certainly need to backfill at least one spot if they trade a starter. They’re already losing Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta to free agency.

Drew Rasmussen is slated to anchor the group. He’s coming off his second straight top 10 Cy Young finish and has stayed healthy for the last two seasons. The Rays exercised a $20MM option on Rasmussen for 2027, the final year of his contract. Neander began the offseason by saying they currently intend to hang onto their ace, who’d make the highest salary in team history.

Assuming that’s the case, the likeliest outcome is that Rasmussen would depart next offseason in free agency. The Rays would presumably receive some kind of compensation, either through the qualifying offer or something similar in the next collective bargaining agreement. However, Neander implied to FanSided’s Robert Murray at the GM Meetings that the Rays would have some interest in extension talks.

Rasmussen is currently slated to hit free agency in his age-32 season. If he stays healthy next year, he could command a three- or four-year deal at $25-30MM annually. That’s not traditionally a Rays move, though they did sign Glasnow to an extension that had a $25MM salary in the final season. (They traded him to the Dodgers before that year.) They don’t have any guaranteed contracts beyond next year and have forecasted a future payroll uptick with the expectation they’ll have a new stadium in the City of Tampa for the 2029 season.

title: ABC and ESPN address concerns over nationwide ground stop delaying college football games
content:

How The FAA Ground Stop Is Affecting CFB, NFL This Weekend
content: The Federal Aviation Administration's decision to ground all flights nationwide Friday threw the sports world into chaos, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time for them to travel to their games this weekend. The FAA issued a notice that said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." At around 8:30 p.m. ET, the FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop. Despite the official notice that the air travel ban was lifted, it doesn't simply revert back to business as usual. Teams and programs across the nation were impacted and continue to be as they try to travel to their games this weekend. For example, No. 18 USC was able to take off before the ban was instituted and reportedly landed for its game in Bloomington against No. 9 Indiana on Saturday at 3:30 p.m. ET. Colorado State, whose flight to Washington State was impacted, used the tarmac as grounds for a walk-through practice. Before the ban was lifted, transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later said there was a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, and that FAA technicians were investigating. "There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said. Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, eighth-ranked Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games. The Utes play at No. 22 Arizona, the Longhorns visit No. 24 LSU and the Vols are traveling to Texas A&M in three of the bigger games of the weekend. In the case of the Longhorns, they posted on social media a short video of them boarding their plane before the stoppage. If they end up taking a bus to Baton Rouge, the trip for the 6:30 p.m. CT kickoff Saturday takes about seven hours. "We are grounded and waiting to see when we can leave," a team spokesman said. Other schools affected by the stoppage included No. 19 Ole Miss, Baylor, Kansas State, Washington and Minnesota. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time. Several teams were able to take off before the stoppage went into effect, including Missouri, which was flying to No. 1 Georgia; Duke, which was traveling to No. 5 Miami; and No. 10 Texas Tech, which was on the way to Oklahoma State. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Royals In Market For Right-Handed Hitting Outfielder
content:
The Royals are looking for a right-handed hitting outfielder, general manager J.J. Picollo told reporters at the GM Meetings this week (link via ESPN’s Jesse Rogers). The GM added that an acquisition would ideally be capable of playing center field on at least a part-time basis.

That’s essentially the role Lane Thomas played for K.C. this year. They picked him up on a one-year, $5.25MM free agent contract last offseason. Thomas played reasonably well for a half-season, batting .232/.326/.393 across 97 games. He started 72 contests in the outfield, 52 of them up the middle. They traded him to Atlanta at the deadline for a pair of minor league pitchers and to dump what remained of Bailey Falter’s arbitration salary.

Thomas didn’t play particularly well for the Braves. He’s back on the market and might be available even more cheaply than he was a year ago if the Royals wanted to reengage. Tyrone Taylor, Myles Straw, Jake Meyers and Victor Robles are other possibilities as fourth/fifth outfield types. If the Royals wanted a potential everyday center fielder, Luis Robert Jr. is the top right-handed hitter on the free agent market.

Dane Myers and Jonny DeLuca are fourth outfielders who could be available on the trade front. The Nationals are fielding interest in former second overall pick Dylan Crews, who’s a change of scenery candidate. Washington will probably be looking for an affordable pitcher in return, though, and that’s not an area of organizational strength for Kansas City. The Royals might balk at giving up Noah Cameron given Crews’ lack of big league production to this point. Players like Luinder Avila (who’ll likely miss next season after August Tommy John surgery) or Daniel Lynch IV don’t seem enticing enough for Washington to part with a player who has Crews’ draft and prospect pedigree.

Kansas City arguably should be looking for two outfield acquisitions. Right fielder Jac Caglianone is their only clear regular. Left fielder Isaac Collins underwhelmed in his first season after being acquired from Milwaukee. Kyle Isbel is a strong defensive center fielder but had a career-worst .224/.268/.323 showing at the plate. He’s in his final year of arbitration control and a potential non-tender candidate on a projected $3.5MM salary (courtesy of MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz). Even if the Royals keep Isbel around, they’d ideally push him into a true fourth outfield role. Tyler Tolbert and John Rave are fifth outfield types.

There’s room on the roster for K.C. to both add a right-handed hitting center fielder like Taylor or Meyers and acquire a true everyday player in left field. Ian Happ, Taylor Ward, Ramón Laureano, and Trent Grisham are free agent possibilities. Former K.C. target Jarren Duran is all but guaranteed to be traded or non-tendered by the Red Sox after they agreed to a four-year deal with Jake Bauers. Brandon Marsh and JJ Bleday are other trade possibilities.

title: Predictions On Who Will Sign MLB's Top Free Agents, Including Tarik Skubal
content: As Brewers manager Pat Murphy walked to the stage at Tropicana Field after winning the World Series, he turned to his head of baseball operations to deliver a message. "Hey, I have some thoughts for spring training in ‘27,’" Matt Arnold recalled Murphy telling him. "I’m like, ‘Not right now. Now’s not the time.’" Amid the revelry, Arnold wanted to take a moment to absorb the present before considering the future. But that time has come now, especially with one of the Brewers’ top sluggers already set to wear a new uniform in 2027. This week’s GM meetings laid the groundwork for what could be a flurry of activity before the collective bargaining agreement ends on the night of Dec. 1. As Major League executives departed Las Vegas on Thursday, the Braves struck a three-year deal for longtime Dodgers reliever Evan Phillips, who returns to the team that drafted him in 2015. Less than 24 hours later, the Red Sox made the biggest move in free agency to this point, signing NLCS MVP Jake Bauers. Boston found the power bat in Bauers, who declined his qualifying offer in Milwaukee and agreed to a four-year, $58 million deal with the Red Sox. Perhaps that catalyzes the market. As of now, nearly every free agent in our Top 50 is still available. Here are 10 of the top players on the market, along with potential landing spots for each. 1. Tarik Skubal, LHP Why He's Ranked Here: Skubal is in a clear tier by himself in this year’s otherwise light free-agent class. His agent, Scott Boras, will look to make him the highest-paid pitcher in the sport’s history, which would require a team surpassing the 12-year, $325 million contract the Dodgers gave to Yoshinobu Yamamoto. It’s no surprise, then, why the New York Mets are considered the favorites to land him. While there will only be a handful of teams willing to shop at this level of the market, it does sound like one of them might pounce before a potential lockout. 2. Michael King, RHP Why He's Ranked Here: King opted out after the first year of his three-year, $75 million contract with the Padres to become a free agent. Clearly, the former reliever would like another multi-year offer after producing a 3.15 ERA over three seasons as a full-time starter in San Diego. His strikeout rate dipped, and his walk rate climbed last year while throwing a career-high 185 innings, but he no longer has a qualifying offer attached to him the way he did last winter. That should make him an especially appealing target on the open market and could yield him a bigger deal than he received last winter. Still, a return to San Diego remains a possibility. His impact on the Padres in October was immeasurable. King allowed one run in 14 postseason innings and was fearless, picking up a save in Game 3 of the NLDS with two scoreless innings of relief just two days after starting Game 2. 3. Randy Arozarena, OF Why He's Ranked Here: Arozarena has produced at least 20 homers and 20 steals in six straight seasons, an especially noteworthy feat considering his last 2 ½ years have been spent in Seattle. As Boras put it: "He’s a model of consistency, and he’s done it in a market where right-handed hitters go to die." Indeed, Arozarena was one of the only bright spots in the Mariners’ disappointing lineup, producing an .865 OPS that represented his highest mark over the course of a full season in his eight-year career. In a market with few right-handed offensive threats, it’ll be interesting to see whether teams value Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki as the better option as both outfield sluggers enter their age-32 seasons. Each player has a qualifying offer attached. 4. Seiya Suzuki, OF Why He's Ranked Here: Overshadowed by MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong in the Cubs’ outfield, Suzuki just put together the most valuable season of his career (5.1 bWAR). It was also his fourth straight season with at least 20 home runs and an OPS over .800. Since joining the Cubs in 2022, Suzuki ranks 12th in MLB in both OPS and wRC+ among all qualified right-handed hitters. For teams seeking a right-handed slugger who won’t hurt them defensively in a corner, he might be the most alluring outfielder on the market. Suzuki’s five outs above average and 14 defensive runs saved last season both represented career highs. Can he replicate that level of defense as he gets deeper into his 30s? 5. Teruaki Sato, 3B/OF Why He's Ranked Here: Sato’s aggressiveness at the plate and questions defensively bring risk, but we’re also talking about a 27-year-old who might be the best bat on the market. He launched 40 home runs in 2025 and another 39 in 2026 for NPB’s Hanshin Tigers. His 79 homers over the last two seasons were 15 more than the next-closest NPB player, and he also won the Triple Crown last season. There will be plenty of teams willing to live with an elevated strikeout rate if the lefty slugger can maintain that power in his move to MLB. Sato may ultimately have to bump from third base to first base or, more likely, a corner outfield spot. But don’t be surprised if he ends up the highest-paid position player in this year’s class. 6. Brandon Lowe, 2B Why He's Ranked Here: Lowe’s contract year in Pittsburgh couldn’t have gone much better. He led all MLB second basemen with 35 home runs, though the power was nothing new. He has hit at least 30 homers three times in his nine-year career, has hit at least 20 homers each of the last four seasons and has been an above-league-average hitter every season. The bigger changes were his defense and durability. Known as a bat-first infielder, Lowe is coming off the best defensive season of his career. He went from minus-14 defensive runs saved and outs above average with the Rays in 2025 to plus-13 and plus-15 in those categories, respectively, in his lone season with the Pirates in 2026. He also played in a career-high 150 games. Teams will have to weigh how much they believe in his improved health and defense as he enters his age-32 season. Either way, second basemen with this kind of power don’t become available often. 7. Luis Arraez, 2B Why He's Ranked Here: Arraez has hit fewer than 10 home runs in seven of his first eight seasons, but his bat-to-ball skills have made him an above league-average hitter every year of his career and a four-time All-Star. Last year, he hit .310 — even after a disappointing finish to the season following a trade from San Francisco to Philadelphia — and came a point away from winning the NL batting crown. More surprisingly, though, he also produced the best defensive season of his career after shifting from first base back to second, where the 29-year-old graded out as a top-five defensive player at his position by outs above average. As teams weigh the sustainability of that dramatic defensive improvement, he at least provided reason to believe he could be more than just an elite contact hitter. 8. Freddy Peralta, RHP Why He's Ranked Here: For a while, Peralta’s walk year looked like a disaster. He had a 4.99 ERA in 22 starts with the Mets before finding refuge in Tampa Bay, where he made some tweaks, found his fastball again and gained his confidence back. Peralta had a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts for the Rays, including a 0.79 ERA over his final six starts of the regular season, before producing a 2.95 ERA over five playoff appearances. Overall, Peralta’s 21.4% strikeout rate last year was the lowest of his career, but his underlying numbers were better than his 4.42 ERA demonstrated, and his late-season uptick combined with a history of production could make the 30-year-old the most desirable starter on the market behind Skubal. 9. Ryan Jeffers, C Why He's Ranked Here: Over the last four seasons, Jeffers’ .782 OPS and 119 wRC+ (19% better than league average) rank eighth among all primary catchers. Last year, his .814 OPS was the second-highest mark of his career and ranked fourth among all catchers with at least 300 plate appearances. You have to decrease the minimum because he only played in 92 games after fracturing his hamate bone. Staying on the field has been an issue for the 29-year-old, who has never played more than 122 games in a single season, and he’s an average defender at best. Still, his bat makes him the clear top catcher on the market and should generate plenty of interest. The Twins gave him the qualifying offer for a reason. Prediction: Minnesota Twins — They decided not to trade him at the deadline; best not to let him walk now, even if he declines the qualifying offer, considering the lack of depth behind him. 10. Clay Holmes, RHP Why He's Ranked Here: The veteran ground-ball extraordinaire looked like an All-Star through his first nine starts last year, producing a 2.39 ERA for the Mets before fracturing his fibula. He was traded to the Cubs at the deadline and looked terrific in August (1.55 ERA in five starts) before falling apart in September (8.24 ERA) with as many walks (15) as strikeouts (15) over his final four starts of the season. While Holmes was limited to 101.1 innings last season, the former All-Star closer has demonstrated his worthiness as a starter, producing a 3.44 ERA over the last two seasons after converting from the bullpen. His ability to pitch in either role should be enticing to any playoff contender. With the highest ground-ball rate of any starter in MLB last season (60.7%), Holmes is best suited somewhere with a good defensive infield behind him. Prediction: Chicago Cubs — It's fair to wonder if his late-season struggles in Chicago — and the fact that the Cubs didn’t pitch him in the wild-card series — might impact his willingness to return. Still, the Cubs’ elite defense and multiple needs in the rotation make Chicago a logical fit.

title: Bill Simmons issues Ringer statement on Van Lathan’s beef with ‘Dan Le Batard Show’ crew: ‘Please give it a big slurp’
content:
Bill Simmons waded into the feud — if you want to call it that — between The Ringer and The Dan Le Batard Show on Friday’s episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast, delivering what he billed as an official company statement in support of Van Lathan, who earlier this week told Le Batard and his cohorts to “suck my d*ck” on the Ringer Tailgate podcast.

Lathan’s rant was a response to a Le Batard Show segment built around a Tailgate clip of Billy Gil, the former Le Batard producer who has long needled University of Miami fans and questioned the Hurricanes’ playoff credentials after their 31-24 loss at Notre Dame.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Ringer Tailgate (@ringertailgate)

In airing the clip, Le Batard’s show trimmed the portion where Lathan and Joel Anderson pushed back on Gil’s take, ridiculed the cast for talking over one another, and capped the bit with Zaslow wondering aloud who these guys were.

Lathan, who, along with Anderson, had previously appeared as a guest on Le Batard’s show, took particular exception to the condescension and to the Le Batard crew pulling him and his cohosts into its history with Gil.

“They took that out to focus on the sh*t that they wanted to nitpick on. Then, they hit us with the white man sh*t. They hit us with the, ‘Who are these people?'” he said.

“Man, I’m gonna be all the way real with y’all. Shout out to everything you got going over there, but y’all not doing it big enough to come at nobody on the ‘Who are you?’ type sh*t. I don’t know what the f*ck y’all think y’all got popping over there that makes you be able to come, especially, talk to us like that.”

The Dan Le Batard Show has always spoken in its own dialect of running gags and inside jokes, much of it indecipherable to anyone who hasn’t logged hundreds of hours with the program, and Zaslow’s “who are these guys” bore every indication of being one of those bits, as feigning ignorance about whoever is on the other side of a clip is a recurring shtick of his.

Unfortunately, a punchline built for the regulars tends to sound more like an insult to the people on the receiving end, and The Le Batard Show has a history of mistaking its own insularity for a feature. Whenever criticism comes its way, the program’s reflexive defense has long been that detractors simply don’t get the show. That argument loses some of its force, though, when the show’s ever-expanding, ever-evolving post-ESPN identity has left even devoted longtime listeners like our Brendon Kleen wondering who, exactly, is supposed to get it.

Bill Simmons, for his part, didn’t seem particularly concerned with getting it. The Ringer founder rehashed the whole saga with Joe House on before delivering what he tongue-in-cheekily presented as the company’s formal stance on the matter.

“Here’s my statement on behalf of The Ringer: We fully support Van’s comments,” Simmons said. “Please give it a big slurp, those guys.”

The Ringer vs. Le Batard show saga continues.

Bill Simmons has stepped in with an “official Ringer statement”: fully supporting Van telling them to “suck my dick” and doesn’t know who Le Batard co-host “Zaslav” is https://t.co/OjMWJV0bzm

— Rob Lopez (@r0bato) November 13, 2026

Chief among “those guys” is Zaslow, though Simmons appears to know him better as “Zaslav.” That would be David Zaslav, the former Warner Bros. Discovery CEO, who, to our knowledge, has yet to weigh in on the Hurricanes’ playoff résumé.

title: The Best Fits For Tarik Skubal
content:
The spotlight is on Tarik Skubal, who is the top free agent of the offseason. He is one of the best pitchers alive right now. He has a 2.64 earned run average over the past four seasons. His 30.1% strikeout rate and 4.8% walk rate in that time are both elite figures. His 44.6% ground ball rate in that span isn’t quite as gaudy but is still better than average. He won the American League Cy Young in both 2024 and 2025.

His 2026 was interrupted by an elbow surgery but he still managed to post a 2.72 ERA over 26 starts, plus two more postseason starts. He was traded midseason, making him ineligible for a qualifying offer. Even if he did have the QO, it would be a minor consideration for a player this talented, but the lack of QO only helps.

Skubal is the best classic, prime-aged starter to hit the market in years. Shohei Ohtani was obviously a special case as a two-way player. In terms of pure pitchers, it’s expected that Skubal’s contract will set new benchmarks in terms of guarantee or average annual value or both. The record in the former category is Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s $325MM deal with the Dodgers. In the latter camp, both Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander got AAVs of $43.33MM late in their careers.

Skubal turns 30 next week. That makes him one year older than Gerrit Cole was when Cole got a nine-year deal from the Yankees seven years ago. But he’s also one year younger than Max Fried was when he got an eight-year deal from the Yanks two years ago. MLBTR predicted Skubal to get to nine years and a total of $425MM, an average annual value of $47.22MM. It wouldn’t be a surprise if Skubal’s representatives at the Boras Corporation set their sights even higher.

Almost every club needs starting pitching but only some of them are realistic fits for that kind of contract. There’s a chance that Skubal’s market doesn’t develop as expected and he pivots to a shorter-term deal with a higher AAV. Several free agents have gone this way over the years, including Kyle Tucker and Bo Bichette last year.

Both Jeff Passan of ESPN and Mark Feinsand of MLB.com have reported that Skubal has no interest in going that direction, but that’s to be expected at this stage. Most players go to free agency looking for the best long-term deal they can find. Pivoting to a short-term pact is usually a back-up plan.

The last time Boras had the top free agent in the class, he got Juan Soto a 15-year deal with the Mets. Soto didn’t have to sacrifice on AAV either. His $51MM AAV was a record at the time, when factoring in the deferrals in Ohtani’s deal. Tucker’s deal a year later passed Soto in the AAV department, though on a much shorter pact.

The possibility of a Tucker-like pivot to a short deal can’t be discounted but it’s probably safe to assume that, like with Soto, Boras will try to get Skubal a strong deal both in terms of length and AAV. Reporting has indicated that Skubal and his reps will be meeting with various suitors in the coming weeks with the hope of getting a deal done before the lockout begins on December 2.

As we do with the top free agents every offseason, we’ll run through each team’s chances of signing Skubal.

All payroll figures cited are from the MLBTR Payroll Tracker, courtesy of contributor Ethan Hullihen.

Known/Likely Suitors (listed alphabetically)

Blue Jays: The Blue Jays have been connected to just about every available marquee player in recent years. They missed on Ohtani and Soto but they signed Dylan Cease to a $210MM deal last offseason. They also reportedly offered Tucker a ten-year, $350MM deal a few months later, before Tucker would pivot to short-term offers from the Mets and Dodgers.

The Jays just had a bunch of money come off the books. Their competitive balance tax number was $317MM this year but they are projected for just $233MM next year. There is room for them to be aggressive. If it’s true that Skubal doesn’t want to go short term, perhaps that gives the Blue Jays an edge, as they were the one team publicly known to offer Tucker a viable long-term pact. The Jays have a meeting scheduled with Skubal but a report this week from Mitch Bannon and Will Sammon of The Athletic downplayed their pursuit a bit.

Toronto certainly needs rotation help. They have a solid front three with Cease, Trey Yesavage and José Soriano but there are lots of questions with their options for the final two spots. If they want to make a big splash after their disappointing 2026 season, signing Skubal would be the most straightforward way to do it.

title: Ian Eagle reveals advice he gave Noah before ‘Sunday Night Football’ fill-in
content:
Before Noah Eagle could tell a national audience he was calling Sunday Night Football, he had to tell his father.

Ian Eagle recounted the whirlwind weekend on Seattle Sports’ Brock and Salk, telling Brock Huard and Mike Salk that shortly after he reached his hotel room in Charlotte, where he was in town to call Sunday’s Broncos-Panthers game for CBS, his phone rang around 11:45, and his son was on the other end of the line. Noah was only hours away from calling Notre Dame-Miami for NBC, and he had just learned that Mike Tirico would be unable to work the Buccaneers-Bears game in Chicago the following night and that the network needed him to step into the chair.

NBC had ruled Tirico out with a health issue, so the call carried a note of unease before it could feel like good news. Tirico is a longtime friend of Ian’s, and the elder Eagle’s first instinct was concern for Tirico’s well-being rather than excitement over the biggest assignment of his son’s career.

“Obviously concern is for Mike at that point, who is a longtime friend and someone that has played a huge role in my life, my career, and [I] have a very deep personal connection with,” Eagle said. “And then you shift your attention, and now you go into dad mode, which is, ‘All right, dude, focus on what’s in front of you. Deal with Notre Dame-Miami. You’ve been spending all week preparing for this game. This is the biggest game of the year for NBC college coverage.'”

Once the paternal pep talk ended, Ian sketched out a blueprint for the next 30 hours. He assumed Noah would leave for Chicago as soon as the South Bend broadcast wrapped and start turning the page on the drive. He suggested broad strokes on Saturday night, heavy reliance on the crew members who had spent the whole week preparing for Bucs-Bears, and a concentrated three-to-four-hour stretch on Sunday to lock in names and numbers.

According to Noah’s own account in an interview with our Drew Lerner, that blueprint closely resembled what actually happened. The 29-year-old drove to Chicago after Notre Dame-Miami, reached his hotel shortly after midnight, and climbed into bed a little past 1 a.m. before waking at 8:30 for a 9 a.m. production meeting. He then devoted roughly four hours to cramming, leaning on Cris Collinsworth, Melissa Stark, producer Rob Hyland, and director Drew Esocoff for their accumulated knowledge of both teams. Tirico also forwarded the preparation he had completed during the week, and Noah’s statistician, Josh Zaleznik, printed his spotting charts at a FedEx on Saturday while Noah finished his college work.

“I really just approached it like, okay, look, I can’t do a standard week’s worth of work. And so as a result of that, I’m not going to overly stress, I’m just going to do my game tonight and then I’m going to do as much as I can leading up on Sunday.

“More than anything, when I got there on Sunday, just hearing from Cris Collinsworth and Melissa Stark, and Rob Hyland, the producer, and Drew Esocoff, the director, and getting their deep dive on the game, that was probably the most helpful thing for me. Just getting an understanding of what they saw through the week in all of their meetings that I obviously wasn’t a part of.

“And then the other part of this is that I had charts made up Saturday once I found out I was gonna do this. My statistician, Josh Zaleznik, went to FedEx and printed them and then brought them to me, because I was still in college mode, finishing all my stuff for Notre Dame-Miami. That was super helpful for me as well, just to save some time.

“A lot of credit to Mike Tirico as well, because he sent me what he had already done through the week. So I got to at least see that, which I thought was very helpful, seeing where he was laying things out.”

Getting Noah ready was only half of Ian’s message. The other half came from more than three decades of calling games, and it pared the job down to the one obligation that matters more than any sleepless night or stack of spotting charts once the red light comes on.

“And then the other part of the thought process for me as a play-by-play guy is a reminder to him of, ‘Hey, you got to nail the big calls,'” Eagle said. “That’s really what it comes down to. Nobody cares about how much sleep you got. Nobody cares about how much prep you’ve done. All they care is when you’re on the air that you are as one with the event. You’re engaged with the event, you’re engaged with your analyst and your sideline reporter, and let the game do its thing.”

Noah, for his part, put a little more stock in sleep than his father’s speech allowed, telling Lerner he protected his rest on Saturday night because he knew he would be dulled once the broadcast began without it. On nearly everything else, father and son were aligned. Noah said he learned early in his career that audiences remember the beginning and end of a broadcast, so he concentrated on a crisp open and a clean finish that could contain whatever chaos unfolded in between. He likened his role to a bus driver responsible for delivering the VIP, in this case Collinsworth, to the right destinations. That deference to his analyst mirrored Ian’s insistence on staying engaged with the people beside him in the booth.

The matchup did him a favor, too. Bucs-Bears blossomed into an improbably wild back-and-forth affair, which Noah said allowed him to settle in and react to each snap rather than lean on season-long storylines he hadn’t had time to study.

“So that’s exactly what I told him, and I think he followed the advice exactly to a T,” the elder Eagle concluded.

Noah’s stint in Tirico’s chair didn’t end in Chicago. Two nights later, he filled in again on Celtics-76ers, and how long NBC will need him to keep covering for its top play-by-play voice is still unclear. Noah told Lerner the weekend left him with conflicted feelings, grateful for the opportunity but uneasy about the reason it came his way. Nobody understands that tug-of-war better than his father, who answered the phone in that Charlotte hotel room as both Tirico’s friend and Noah’s dad.

title: Angels, Tyler Heineman Avoid Arbitration
content:
The Angels announced that they have signed catcher Tyler Heineman to a one-year deal for the 2027 season worth $1.2375MM. They also re-signed left-hander Sammy Peralta via a minor league contract with an invitation to spring training.

Heineman, 36 in June, is a journeyman catcher. He has played for the Marlins, Giants, Blue Jays, Pirates, Red Sox and Angels in his career. He had a really nice season with the Jays in 2025, backing up Alejandro Kirk. Heineman hit .289/.361/.416 in 174 plate appearances. He also got strong grades for his work behind the plate. FanGraphs credited him with 2.1 wins above replacement. He got into a couple of postseason games as the Jays made a World Series run.

Though he was 34 years old, he qualified for arbitration for the first time after that season. The Jays tendered him a contract for his age-35 season and the two sides avoided a hearing by agreeing to a salary of $1.2375. Unfortunately, he couldn’t carry things over into 2026. While Kirk was on the injured list, the Jays called up Brandon Valenzuela to share the catching duties with Heineman. Valenzuela played well as Heineman struggled. Heineman is out of options so he was designated for assignment when Kirk came off the IL.

Heineman was traded to the Angels for cash but struggled with his new club as well. He finished the season with a .175/.223/.220 batting line. Part of that was due to a .205 batting average on balls in play but his walk rate also dropped from last year’s 6.9%, which was already a subpar figure, to just 2.5% this year. That was the lowest walk rate of any hitter who made at least 160 plate appearances this year.

After that dismal showing, Heineman was a non-tender candidate going into 2027. Salaries almost never go down via the arbitration system. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projected him for a modest raise to $1.5MM. It’s common for deals signed before the non-tender deadline to come in under projections. This is because a team will effectively say “take it or leave it” to a player at risk of being non-tendered. Heineman has agreed to make the same salary next year as he did this season.

Though he didn’t hit much in 2026, Heineman’s glovework still got strong marks. Statcast gave him above-average grades for his framing and work with the running game, while having him league average with blocking. As of now, the Angels project to have Moisés Ballesteros and Heineman as their catching duo. Ballesteros is unproven at the big league level but he was a bat-first prospect. Heineman can perhaps serve as a veteran mentor and glove-first backup but it’s also possible the Angels make more moves before Opening Day 2027.

The club doesn’t even have a proper front office leader yet. John Mozeliak is guiding things right now as the team waits for MLB approval of the sale from Arte Moreno to Stan Kroenke. In time, more clarity might emerge on the club’s plans. For now, they have opted for status quo.

Peralta, 29 in May, was outrighted off the roster at season’s end. He elected free agency but has circled back to the Halos a few weeks later. He has a 5.64 earned run average in 68 2/3 major league innings. He has occasionally shown some potential in the minors. In 241 Triple-A innings over the past four years, he has a 23% strikeout rate and 6.8% walk rate. That has nonetheless resulted in a 5.08 ERA, thanks in part to an unlucky 61.5% strand rate. His 4.43 FIP in that time is a bit more optimistic.

The Halos have a fairly wide open bullpen at the moment. Only Tayler Saucedo, Ben Joyce and Sam Bachman have qualified for arbitration. Every other reliever on the roster in his pre-arb years. It’s therefore a decent landing spot for Peralta. If he makes the roster at any point next year, he is out of options.

title: Sean McVay Gives Injury Updates On Rams Stars Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie
content: Los Angeles Rams defensive end Myles Garrett expects to play Sunday despite missing practice, while cornerback Trent McDuffie is questionable for their game at the Arizona Cardinals. Garrett was held out of practice on Friday after being limited earlier in the week because of a knee injury that caused him to miss seven games before returning to make three sacks with a forced fumble in the Rams’ 20-13 win at the Washington Commanders on Sunday. "He’s had a really good week," coach Sean McVay said. "Played a bunch of snaps, and expect him to be able to build on that. But we’re being smart with him." Garrett was largely pleased with his performance, in which he played 61.5% of the defensive snaps, apart from needing to build up his endurance and address what he felt was a slow get-off time. "I'm sure Next Gen or PFF or somebody would tell me it wasn't too bad," Garrett said. "It felt terrible to me." McDuffie is dealing with a back injury that forced him to miss the Rams’ third straight win last week, getting them over .500 for the first time this season at 5-4. McVay expressed optimism he would be able to play, provided McDuffie felt good coming out of Friday's workout. "He was rolling, you know, doing a lot of good stuff yesterday," McVay said. The ongoing issues with the Rams’ two marquee offseason acquisitions are indicative of their larger injury crisis that has threatened a campaign that began with them as Super Bowl betting favorites. Los Angeles is so beat up that star wide receiver Puka Nacua was placed on injured reserve Thursday to free up a roster spot, a reversal from what McVay had indicated earlier in the week when he cited the limited number of IR slots remaining to be able to bring players back later in the season. "Some things changed where we needed that spot because of all the moving pieces," said McVay, while adding that nothing has changed with the timeline for Nacua’s return from knee and toe injuries. Safety Kam Curl is questionable with a toe injury, but McVay indicated he is likely to play. The same is expected for the Rams’ banged-up crop of tight ends, Colby Parkinson (ribs), Tyler Higbee (illness) and Davis Allen (oblique). All three are needed to supplement the passing game with top receivers Nacua, Davante Adams (hamstring) and Jordan Whittington (back) on IR. Tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring) and left guard Steve Avila (hamstring) were ruled officially out, as was previously announced. The Rams were upset by the Cardinals 18-16 on Oct. 18, giving up a last-minute drive which ended with Chad Ryland kicking his sixth field goal as time expired at SoFi Stadium. Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: Dutch Romp Greece, Germany Cruises In UEFA Nations League Action
content: The Netherlands routed Greece 7-0 in a statement Nations League victory to stay unbeaten under new coach Xavi, while Jürgen Klopp's Germany cruised to a 3-1 win over Serbia on Friday. That now sets up a decider between the two big-name coaches for first place in their group. Tijjani Reijnders scored a hat trick and Jurrien Timber had two goals in a rampant win for the Netherlands. Beaming and holding up three fingers, Reijnders celebrated a hat trick which came off a series of slick team moves to tear apart the Greek defense in Amsterdam. Crysencio Summerville got the Netherlands started with a sixth-minute opener before Reijnders scored three in the space of 21 minutes, Timber added two more and Donyell Malen a seventh. Germany is three points behind Group A2 leader the Netherlands before they play on Monday in Berlin. The top two in the group advance to the quarterfinals, with head-to-head record as the tiebreaker. The Netherlands, Germany and Greece are all able to qualify. Serbia is last after losing all of its five games. Germany Wins In Front Of Serbia's Sparse Crowd Goals from Florian Wirtz and debutant Brajan Gruda lifted Germany to its second win in five games with Klopp as coach after a slow start to his tenure. In driving rain, Germany was ahead after just three minutes when Serbia defender Srdjan Babic turned Germany forward Kai Havertz’s header into his own goal. It was 2-0 soon after when Wirtz flicked a rebound over goalkeeper Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, who had parried a shot from Havertz. Klopp’s experimental squad, with Freiburg winger Derry Scherhant but no place for Barcelona’s Karim Adeyemi, added a third when Leipzig's Gruda dribbled through the center of the Serbian defense to score Germany’s third. Babic canceled out his earlier own goal by scoring for Serbia on a rebound, but chances of a comeback were ended when Vanja Dragojevic was sent off for a reckless tackle on Joshua Kimmich's ankle. The 50,000-capacity Rajko Mitic stadium was almost empty because Serbia was supported by only 5,000 accompanied children and teenagers. That's because UEFA was punished the Serbian soccer federation for fans’ offensive behavior in the previous rounds. Swiss Promotion Bid On Track Switzerland is playing in the second tier of the Nations League for the first time, but its bid to rejoin Europe's elite stayed on course in a 0-0 draw with Slovenia, its closest rival in Group B1. Scotland won against North Macedonia 2-1. Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: Stephen A. Smith ‘feels presidential’ after Donald Trump interview: ‘I belong here’
content:
Stephen A. Smith entered the White House to interview Donald Trump as a podcast host, and he left feeling presidential.

The once-growing belief that the ESPN host will eventually run for president has faded in the last year or so. Partly because Smith has insisted he will not give up his highly lucrative media gigs, and partly because he’s built a political platform without being transparent about where he stands on many issues.

To Smith’s credit, his political platform landed him at the White House twice in the last month. After joining Bill Maher and Kid Rock for a dinner with Trump at the White House several weeks ago, Smith returned this week to interview the president for his YouTube show. And while reflecting on the interview during a segment with Skip Bayless on his SiriusXM Radio show Friday afternoon, Smith admitted his latest visit to the White House has him feeling like he belongs there.

“Once I was leaving, I don’t even know if I should admit this on the air, but it’s true. I kind of felt like I could be here, like I could do this,” Smith told Bayless.

As he left the White House, reporters closed in on Smith to take pictures and get comments before he was ushered over to a designated stakeout position to answer questions. And in that moment, Smith really began to feel in his element.

“I felt kinda presidential. I really really did. I was like, this is kinda cool,” Smith said on his Mad Dog Sports Radio show. “I wasn’t scared to answer any questions. And then Trump’s staff came running out to get me away from there. I’m thinking they didn’t want me talking until the interview came out. I come to find out once I had left, they were trying to get me out of there so I didn’t have to talk to the media cause they thought I minded. And I didn’t mind at all.”

“I departed outside looking at the backdrop of the White House feeling like, ‘Yeah, I kind of belong here. I think I can do this.’”

While Smith maintains he could win a presidential election, he also claims wading into the political waters in recent years has rekindled his love for covering sports.

“I do believe that I could win the presidency if I ran, Smith insisted to Bayless. “I genuinely believe I could win the presidency. But here’s the thing…the more I do it, the more I’ve fallen in love with sports. I love doing this radio show. I love doing First Take. I love talking about sports. As much as I’ve loved doing what I’ve done for decades, this experience in the world of politics has made me love sports even more.”

Smith has been criticized for being too soft during the interview with Trump. But he is a sports personality interviewing one of the most polarizing and divisive presidents in United States history.

The question should be: why is Stephen A. Smith interviewing the president about politics, rather than why didn’t Stephen A. Smith do a better job interviewing the president? Smith explained he was focused on balancing tough questions with not wanting Trump to walk out of the interview. Although if you’re looking for clicks and engagement, Trump storming out of an interview might have set records.

Recognizing he covers sports for a living, Smith said it’s not his mission to fact-check or debate when interviewing Trump or any political figure. Instead, he tries to get answers that can then be assessed and analyzed by political pundits.

title: Jake Bauers Signs With Red Sox: What's Next For Brewers And Free-Agent Market
content: Two years ago, first baseman Jake Bauers nearly retired. On Friday, he agreed to a four-year, $58 million contract with the Red Sox, according to multiple reports. It’s the richest contract of his turbulent career, and the capstone to the best season of his life. And he can paint the town red knowing he gets to keep his health insurance. Bauers seriously considered retiring from Major League Baseball after the 2024 season. The Brewers had just removed Bauers from the 40-man roster and he elected free agency. There wasn’t much interest in Bauers around the league. Up until that point, he was a career .208/.302/.361 hitter with a negative WAR. At 29 years old, Bauers was a journeyman. He'd shuffled across seven organizations, was traded four times, and was designated for assignment once. So Bauers called his agent, told him he was done playing, and planned to become a stay-at-home dad. Life had other plans. In that same offseason, Bauers’ wife, Lauren, was pregnant with their second child. Needing health insurance for their growing family, Bauers decided to sign a minor-league deal with the Brewers. After an encouraging 2025 season in Milwaukee, Bauers fully broke out in a dream season for the 2026 championship Brewers. He led the team with 26 home runs, slashed .266/.389/.484, posted a 140 OPS+ and came up clutch several times throughout the postseason, eventually winning NLCS MVP for his star performance en route to lifting the World Series trophy. Now, he’s an integral part of Boston’s championship dreams. Let’s dive into what’s next for the Red Sox, the Brewers, and the rest of the free-agent market. If there was one thing the Red Sox needed to improve this offseason, it was slug. Boston ranked 26th in home runs and 20th in slugging percentage last season. After trading slugger Rafael Devers to the Giants, the Red Sox’ 2026 lineup was far too reliant on first baseman Willson Contreras to provide power, and now Bauers will help boost those offensive numbers. Speaking of Contreras, where will he play? It seems most likely that the Red Sox will split designated hitter and first base duties between Bauers and Contreras, with the former’s left-handed bat complementing the latter’s right-handed power. Even with that solution, there is still a surplus at DH on the roster. Masataka Yoshida filled that role for the Red Sox last year, taking at-bats as a DH in 67 of the 87 games he logged. He played just seven games in left field. Boston is also set in the outfield, with Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, and Ceddanne Rafaela patrolling the diamond. The Red Sox have floated Duran’s name in recent trade deadlines, and it’s possible they’ll look to move him again this winter. But, if Boston is trying to move Yoshida this offseason to clear up space, it’s likely to be difficult. The 33-year-old is entering the final year of his five-year deal, and he’s owed nearly $20 million in 2027. Yoshida, a lefty-swinging bat, is not exactly sought after on the market. Craig Breslow, Boston’s president of baseball operations, still has plenty of work ahead of him this offseason. Signing Bauers is just the first major move of their winter. And give credit to Breslow & Co. for getting the deal done before the expected lockout after Dec. 1. Bauers gives the Red Sox the clarity they needed to bulk up their offense. The Brewers offered Bauers a one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer after his breakout season in Milwaukee. As recently as this week, during the GM Meetings in Las Vegas, Brewers brass had no idea which way the situation with their stellar first baseman would unfold. "He meant a lot to our group, and he’s a great story," Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told FOX Sports this week. "The family’s unbelievable. It’s really neat. I just want whatever’s best for Jake. He’s a really, really good person." Now that Bauers rejected the qualifying offer, Milwaukee will receive a compensation pick between the end of the first round and the start of Competitive Balance Round A in the 2027 Draft. Still, that compensation hardly lessens the sting of losing Bauers, who became a fan-favorite and a key clubhouse voice with his leadership. Milwaukee’s biggest need this offseason is replenishing the power that Bauers took with him to Boston. Last season, left fielder Jackson Chourio finished second on the team in home runs (25) behind Bauers, with Brice Turang (21) and William Contreras (18) behind him. The Brewers don’t need power to win the division and lead the majors in wins. Last season, they accomplished both feats while recording the second-lowest home runs (154) in the big leagues. But clutch home runs are what helped them defeat the Dodgers in the NLCS. Milwaukee led all playoff teams with 13 homers this October. The Brewers are expected to fill the hole at first base with internal options. The leading candidate is Andrew Vaughn, who could take over at the corner infield spot next year, while top prospect Andrew Fischer, who could be the long-term answer, completes his development in the minors. Another future first-base option could be prospect Blake Burke, who finished last season at Triple-A but isn’t quite ready just yet. Vaughn, 28, does look ready to take over as the club’s everyday first baseman. He hit .306/.390/.444 (130 OPS+) in 104 games for the Brewers last season. In the end, Bauers’ decision to leave Milwaukee shouldn’t change the Brewers’ offseason plans all that much. They knew they probably couldn’t afford to keep Bauers, who chose long-term stability over a one-year deal, and they don’t fault him for it. Arnold said this week, "We’re not that far removed from winning, but also we have to spend the time to assess that." They’ll look to continue supplementing their roster needs in hopes of repeating as world champions in 2027. MLB executives remain compelled to try and get deals done before the sport's Collective Bargaining Agreement expires on Dec. 1. Within the industry, there is talk of a free-agency frenzy expected in the next two weeks to close out the month. Bauers is a huge bat off the board early, and contenders who are aiming to beef up at first base will have to pivot to the next best option. First baseman Ty France, 32, is now the best first baseman available after Bauers signed with the Red Sox. France was one of the best signings of the year for the Padres, who inked him to a one-year minor-league deal for 2026. France significantly outperformed his contract by hitting .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 home runs, 72 RBI and 37 walks across 133 games for San Diego while also excelling defensively at first base. France, of course, is looking for a multi-year deal after his strong season, and he shouldn’t have a problem finding one. Many around the sport continue to expect top free-agent starter Tarik Skubal to sign before the expected lockout, with the New York Mets remaining the favorites — in terms of financial might and starting pitching needs — to sign him. Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns indicated this week at the GM Meetings that the club is also looking to add at first base. They would prefer a right-handed bat, and France could be the answer.

title: Cardinals Reportedly Turned Away Trade Interest In Burleson, Winn
content:
The Cardinals are fielding calls on a lot of players on their roster. Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports that the Cards have received interested in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, shortstop Masyn Winn and first baseman Alec Burleson, though Goold notes that the club quickly turned away the interest in both Winn and Burleson.

It’s not surprising that the phone would ring. The Cardinals have been in seller mode for a while. Last offseason, they traded away Sonny Gray, Nolan Arenado, Willson Contreras and Brendan Donovan to clear payroll and make room for younger players. At this year’s deadline, they traded away Dustin May, JoJo Romero and Lars Nootbaar. Those pitchers were all impending free agents while each position player was under club control through at least 2027.

With all that selling, it’s understandable that clubs with needs would keep the lines open. The Cards seem to be planning for 2027 to be another evaluation year, so players nearing free agency would be logical trade candidates.

Burleson is under club control through 2028. The Cards could emerge as legitimate contenders in that time frame but it’s unclear how aggressively they plan to tackle things in that window. He just hit 26 home runs this year and slashed .279/.343/.473, so now would be a good time to sell high.

MLBTR placed Burleson in the #10 spot on our list of the Top 40 Trade Candidates entering the winter.  MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects Burleson for an $8.3MM salary next year and he would be due another raise for 2028. The Cards don’t have to trade him now but his value will likely only go down from here as his window of club control shrinks and his salary increases. There’s also the chance of him suffering a notable injury or having a dip in performance. As mentioned, he is coming off a good season, so his stock is up.

However, if the Cards are turning down interest, then perhaps they are planning to hold him to see if the 2027 club emerges as a contender. If he stays healthy and productive but the team falls out of the race, they could give more serious consideration to a trade at next year’s deadline or in the subsequent offseason. Then again, a stronger offer later in the offseason could perhaps compel them to change their minds.

Winn’s situation is slightly different. He is still under club control for another three years, so it’s much more likely the Cards are contending in his window. However, they could have considered it anyway. JJ Wetherholt came up as a shortstop prospect. He mostly played second base this year in deference to Winn and had a good season. He was about league average at the plate with strong defense and baserunning. In theory, the Cards could have traded Winn and moved Wetherholt over to short.

This winter’s shortstop market is weak, with no real everyday options available in free agency. The Cards would surely have lots of interest if they put Winn out there. They then could have found a second base replacement, either from within the system or on the open market. But given the framing here, it doesn’t seem as though they have much interest in pursuing that kind of plan, unless the get a better offer in the coming weeks and months.

Trading a catcher is much more likely. The Cards simply have too many options back there. It seems they plan to have Leo Bernal be their top option in 2027. Top prospect Rainiel Rodriguez will likely be in Triple-A next year and knocking on the door. That leaves Iván Herrera, Crooks and Pages as potential trade chips. Herrera’s value is complicated. He’s a solid hitter but he’s one of the worst catchers in the league at controlling the running game. He might be destined to be a designated hitter who catches only occasionally.

Crooks and Pagés are more legitimate backstops and should be of interest to other clubs. Crooks got some Top 100 prospect attention on his way up the ladder. He is considered a strong defender but his bat is more questionable. He draws walks and hits some home runs but strikes out a lot.

In 666 Triple-A plate appearances thus far, he has 29 home runs, an 11.3% walk rate, a .283/.371/.484 line and 125 wRC+ but a high 27.2% strikeout rate. In 195 big league plate appearances, he has a 33.3% strikeout rate and dismal .168/.231/.313 line. The pedigree should lead to trade interest but he’s not proven at the big league level yet. Pagés would likely be viewed as a more straightforward glove-first backup. He has strong defensive grades but has only hit .229/.275/.354 in his career.

Goold also reports that the Cards are trying to suss out the trade value of infielder Nolan Gorman before next week’s non-tender deadline. Gorman has clear power but strikes out way too much. He’s coming off a dismal .184/.272/.308 showing this year. He is projected for a $3.4MM salary next year, which isn’t too appetizing on the heels of that 2026 season.

There’s theoretically a bit of upside because he has an extra year of club control and hit 27 homers back in 2023. With a weak free agent market for third baseman, perhaps someone takes a flier but it wouldn’t be a shock to see him eventually non-tendered.

Elsewhere, Goold notes the Cards have some interest in adding veteran arms to the pitching staff. He specifically mentions Tim Hill and old friend Andrew Kittredge as a couple of guys on the club’s radar. As the Cards have been rebuilding in recent years, they have usually signed some vets to short-term deals to patch up the staff and potentially flip those players later. May, Phil Maton and Ryne Stanek are some guys they have inked in this manner.

Hill just posted a 4.60 earned run average with the Yankees. He doesn’t get huge strikeouts but generates weak contact and grounders. His 68.8% ground ball rate this year was the lowest of anyone who pitched at least four innings. Kittredge has a more balanced approach. He usually gets grounders and strikeouts at an above-average rate. His strikeouts declined in 2026 but he still managed to post a 3.64 ERA. Both pitchers will turn 37 soon and shouldn’t be too costly.

Speaking of May, there’s been some speculation that the Cards could re-sign him and try to redo their 2026. The Cards gave him a $12.5MM deal and a rotation spot then flipped him and Romero to the Brewers for prospects. Goold writes that a reunion for 2027 is not expected as the Cards will probably look to find a similar outcome with a different pitcher. He mentions Kris Bubic as a speculative fit. Like May, Bubic has flashed talent but has also been very injury prone, so it’s a fair comp.
