title: Zach Gelb returns to Audacy as brand manager of Miami’s 104.3 WQAM
content:
Zach Gelb has landed plenty of big gets over the years, but none quite like an entire radio station.

Audacy announced Thursday that Gelb has been named brand manager of 104.3 WQAM in Miami, handing the veteran sports talk host oversight of the station’s content strategy, talent, operations, and branding. The role puts him at the helm of WQAM’s flagship coverage of the Florida Panthers, Miami Heat, Miami Marlins, and the University of Miami Hurricanes’ football and men’s basketball programs.

“I’m honored and elated for the opportunity to help lead WQAM, a legendary sports station that I have great respect for and have been listening to for years,” Gelb said in a statement. “I’m excited to build our next chapter with this incredible staff and deepen our connection with our passionate South Florida fanbase. I’m grateful to Chris Olivero, Jeff Sottolano, Claudia Menegus, Chris Kinard and everyone at Audacy for their belief in me. I am beyond ready to take this new, exciting step in my career.”

A Temple alum, Gelb got his start at WNJE in New Jersey in 2016, pulling double duty as the station’s programming chief and an on-air host for two years.

In March 2018, he made the leap to national radio at CBS Sports Radio, starting out on weekend overnights and steadily climbing the network’s schedule. A December 2023 lineup shakeup eventually landed him the coveted 3-6 p.m. ET afternoon drive slot, which he anchored beginning in January 2024 and through the network’s rebrand as Infinity Sports Network a few months later. Along the way, Gelb also hosted on Audacy’s WFAN in New York, SportsRadio 94WIP in Philadelphia, and WEEI in Boston.

Over his time in afternoon drive, The Zach Gelb Show became an essential stop for the sports world’s biggest voices, producing Mike Mayock’s warning that Tom Brady would eventually have to choose between the broadcast booth and his Raiders ownership stake, Scott Hanson’s pitch to host a college football version of RedZone, and Dan Lanning’s reply to Penn State athletic director Pat Kraft branding Oregon “frauds”. Gelb also broke significant news last fall, reporting that Urban Meyer had “great interest” in Penn State’s head coaching vacancy before NIL concerns scuttled the discussions. When Meyer publicly denied the report, Gelb remained steadfast in his reporting and even challenged the former Ohio State coach to take a lie detector test.

That nearly eight-year run concluded in December 2025, when Westwood One and Audacy rebranded Infinity Sports Network as Westwood One Sports. Gelb resurfaced the following month with a weekday afternoon program on 365 Sports and Rogue Media Network, then added a studio hosting role at Compass Media Networks covering NFL and NCAA football and basketball broadcasts.

Gelb will remain with Compass and is expected to continue the weekly segment he has done with WQAM’s Hoch, Crowder and Solana since 2021, but his new position is purely managerial. He has no plans to host a show of his own, since doing so would require offering unfiltered opinions about the same franchises he’ll now work with directly as the station’s point person.

The 32-year-old has filled in as a WQAM host throughout this year, and he could still step behind the microphone in a pinch. Otherwise, after working his way through nearly every daypart on national radio, he’ll decide who earns those hours in Miami.

title: That Was Fast! Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell Reveals Kirk Cousins Timeline
content: That didn't take long! Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell revealed in a press conference on Friday afternoon that recently acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins will start in the team's Week 10 road matchup against the Green Bay Packers (1 p.m. ET on FOX); the Vikings defeated the Packers at home in Week 1, scoring 29 consecutive points to get a 39-22 victory. "I cannot give him enough credit for coming in here with how he's gone about the week, both him and the coaching staff getting him ready to go, working extremely hard, using all the time we possibly can," O'Connell said of Cousins. "It's been really impressive what he's been able to do with the command and just getting right back in the huddle with a lot of guys he's played with, but certainly some guys he hasn't. "And it's been something that everybody's been very, very impressed with, so exciting to start Kirk." Of course, Cousins' arrival in Minneapolis marks his second stint with the Vikings, as the four-time Pro Bowler played for the franchise from 2018-23 and for O'Connell from 2022-23. Minnesota acquired the 38-year-old Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders on Tuesday afternoon for a 2027 third-round pick. Across the nine starts he made for the Raiders this season, Cousins totaled 2,340 passing yards, 20 passing touchdowns, eight interceptions and a 97.1 passer rating, while completing 64.1% of his passes. After starting the season 0-6, the Vikings have lost back-to-back games. In the second of those two losses, a 23-6 defeat at home on Monday night against the Buffalo Bills, Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz tossed two interceptions, threw for only 81 yards and completed just eight passes. Wentz was starting in place of Kyler Murray, who's dealing with a hamstring strain and will be inactive Sunday, per O'Connell. The Vikings also have quarterback Max Brosmer, who took over for Wentz late in the fourth quarter on Monday night.

Donovan Mitchell fires back at Charles Barkley’s Cavaliers criticism: ‘Who gives a f*ck?’
content:
If Charles Barkley does retire from television after this season on Inside the NBA, don’t expect Cleveland Cavaliers All-Star Donovan Mitchell to be too upset about it.

Prior to their win over the defending champion New York Knicks earlier this week, Barkley gave a very blunt assessment of the Cavaliers on ESPN.

“Man, the Cavs suck.”

Charles Barkley and @realchriswebber share their thoughts on the differences between last year’s and this year’s Cavs teams https://t.co/npXHnhBORs

— NBA on ESPN (@ESPNNBA) November 11, 2026

“Man, the Cavs suck,” Barkley ranted about the Cavaliers, who were 5-6 and struggling to find much rhythm at the time.

Last season, Barkley thought the Cavaliers would win a championship. This season, Barkley thought it was “insanity” for them to run it back after consecutive disappointing playoff exits.

It’s one thing to say they’re not going to win a title with their current roster, but claiming they “suck” seems a bit extreme. The Cavs are running it back with a team that was in the Conference Finals last season. This isn’t a team that missed the playoffs and decided to try again with the same players.

Mitchell eventually learned about Barkley’s rant some time after Cleveland beat the Knicks 115-107 Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden. And Mitchell quickly made it clear he doesn’t think much of Barkley’s analysis.

“Who gives a f*ck?” Mitchell told Chris Fedor of Cleveland.com with a chuckle. “Chuck ain’t here. If Chuck said we were the defending champs and made positive comments, what’s that going to do for us?

“Chuck ain’t doing nothing for us in this locker room. I have nothing but respect for those guys. So, no disrespect to them or you or anyone else, but who gives a f*ck?” Mitchell continued. “At the end of the day, it’s all about us in here.”

Barkley is an excellent TV personality and has been a great ambassador for the NBA since retiring from playing more than a quarter-century ago. But roster analysis and prognostications have never been his strong suit. So if Barkley is saying a team with championship expectations “sucks” after 11 games, then maybe he’s more like those “idiots and fools” on TV he loves to complain about than he realizes.

title: Chiefs RB Walker III Misses Practice With Groin Injury, Sunday Status Unclear
content: Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III missed practice Friday with a sore groin, leaving his status in question for this weekend’s trip to Atlanta, while wide receiver Josh Downs intends to play days after he was acquired in a trade with Indianapolis. Chiefs coach Andy Reid said Walker had "tweaked" his groin and that the team would monitor him leading into Sunday. "We’ll see. He’s not one to say something like that (without meaning it)," Reid said. Walker has run for 872 yards in his first season with Kansas City, leaving him just eight yards behind Bijan Robinson for the NFL lead, though he has played one game fewer than the Atlanta Falcons running back. Walker’s average of 109 yards per game tops the league. Walker also has been instrumental in the passing game, catching 22 balls for 172 yards and four touchdowns. If he’s unable to play this weekend, rookie Emmett Johnson would be in line to carry a bigger load. The fifth-round pick out of Nebraska has provided a breather for Walker most of the season, and he’s shined when given the opportunity. Johnson has 111 yards rushing and a touchdown on just 26 carries, and he has caught 14 passes for 237 yards and another score. "He’s going to play anyway, whether Ken’s there or not," Reid said. "Everybody has confidence in him." Meanwhile, the Chiefs expect to have wide receiver Xavier Worthy available after he left in the second half of last week’s win over the New York Jets with a hamstring injury. That should take a little pressure off Downs, whom the Chiefs acquired from the Indianapolis Colts just before the NFL trade deadline Tuesday in an attempt to build out their depth at the position. The Chiefs already are without wide receiver Tyquan Thornton, who is on injured reserve with a dislocated ankle. "I thought he did a nice job for what we asked him to do, to digest everything in a couple days," Reid said of Downs. "He’s a smart kid and knows how to play. He’s been playing, which is great, and playing at a high level. He worked into the things we asked him to do and did well. I think he’s ready to play in a game for us." Downs had 33 catches for 354 yards and a touchdown in nine games with Indianapolis. The Chiefs expect to have first-round pick Mansoor Delane back after the cornerback missed a couple of games with a shoulder injury, though they likely will be without right tackle Jaylon Moore because of an ankle injury and Peter Woods due to a neck injury. Joshua Ezeudu played well in Moore’s place in last week’s win over the Jets. "Yeah man, again, it’s a next-man-up mentality. It’s the NFL. Any sporting team, that’s what happens," offensive guard Trey Smith said. "Football has a 100 percent injury rate." Reporting by The Associated Press.

title: NFL Trade Deadline: Who Were Biggest Winners, Losers? League Execs React To Top Deals
content: NFL trade deadline day didn't spark a ton of fireworks, but plenty of fireworks were shot off in the days and weeks leading up to Tuesday. Of the deals that were made on deadline day, though, none were bigger than the Minnesota Vikings' decision to reunite with Kirk Cousins. The Vikings gave up a third-round pick to land Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders as their quarterback struggles were clearly holding them back. Other moves, like the massive trades the Jacksonville Jaguars made on Monday or the deal the Chicago Bears swung two weeks ago, could define this season's homestretch and postseason. And on the flip side, the Indianapolis Colts and Philadelphia Eagles waved the white flag on the season, securing major draft capital. So, what should we make of the biggest trade deadline deals? Who won and lost the trade deadline? We asked those questions to general managers, executives and scouts around the league. Here's what we learned. Eric D. Williams: While giving Minnesota props for securing a quality quarterback at the trade deadline, an NFL contract negotiator also questioned the team’s personnel department in evaluating previous quarterback decisions and their fit in head coach Kevin O’Connell’s system. "It’s crazy how expectations can spiral so quickly," the league source told me. "And I mean this more so in regard to Kyler Murray. Going into the season, the expectation was that Kyler was the high-ceiling QB who could return O’Connell’s offense to prominence. But from a pro scouting standpoint, the Minnesota front office clearly missed. And now they’re without a third-round pick. "Good for them for cutting their losses and acquiring Cousins, but it’s clear that the Murray signing [while not costing them hardly any money] was a swing and a miss." The contract negotiator sees Cousins as a clear upgrade, but questioned whether the 38-year-old can stay healthy enough to help lead the Vikings on a deep postseason run, considering his past injury history. "I’m not going to discredit what Cousins can do for Minnesota," the league source told me. "With how that defense is playing, Cousins’ acquisition could also fall in the ‘shooting our shot’ bucket. "They just need him to be competent in KOC’s offense. They don’t need him to play hero ball. If he can just run the offense, then they’ll have a chance. But yes, health is a concern." Another league source told me Daniel Jones would have been a better fit if available, but overall liked the trade. "I wish they could have picked up Daniel, but I understand their thinking," the league source said. "And if the MNF game had gone well, they would not have done anything." Ralph Vacchiano: For the most part, this is being viewed as a classic win-win trade, to varying degrees. For the Vikings, the win is obvious: They found what might be the perfect starting QB for them, and it "only" cost them a third-round pick. "I mean, they were desperate," one NFL general manager told me. "They were calling everybody. And they had to do it. [Kyler] Murray and [Carson] Wentz had been terrible. They were going to cost them a real chance at a Super Bowl. I would’ve held out for a second, at least, and I think they would’ve had to pay it. They weren’t coming out of this without a quarterback." They also got what another NFL executive told me was the "perfect guy for them" — a former Viking who knows Kevin O’Connell’s offense and No. 1 wide receiver Justin Jefferson and won’t need long to get up to speed. "If you think about it, it’s kind of a miracle," the executive told me. "The right guy at the right price, and he’s available halfway through the season. What are the odds it works out like that?" As for the Raiders, the general manager summed up their win like this: "They got a 3 for a guy they were going to bench soon anyway. Maybe they have to turn to Fernando Mendoza (their rookie No. 1 overall pick) a little earlier than they wanted. But it was coming soon anyway. Their future is the kid, not the old man. And now they got a Day 2 pick to help the rebuild, too." Williams: Both league sources I spoke with about Taylor being on the trade market were not surprised the elite running back stayed in Indianapolis. "I don’t know why the Colts would have traded Taylor at all unless they received a crazy offer," an NFL agent told me. "A new GM and coach would want him. He is 27 and under contract for two years. He just did an extension, so trading him borders on asinine. The Colts could get going the rest of the way. The schedule is reasonable to do so." Another league source I talked with believes the Colts are holding Taylor hostage by keeping him on a losing roster that’s tanking the rest of the season. "People lose sight that the players in the locker room are humans," the league source told me. "With everything over the last two weeks pointing to Taylor moving on and him effectively saying his goodbyes after their last game, it was the absolute wrong thing for them to do by not moving him. "I’m hoping he comes up with a mysterious injury that puts him on IR for the rest of the season, and then they move him in the offseason. That would be the right thing to do." Vacchiano: I thought the Colts made the right decision, but I didn’t find many people who agreed with me. Most of my sources saw the decision as a "surprise," and they believed the Colts were going to take the best offer they had, which was believed to be a second-round pick plus a fourth- or fifth-round pick too. "That’s a good deal for a running back," one NFL source told me. "They are in a total rebuild. They sold a bunch of their best players. They have huge questions about their offensive line and quarterback. They’re going to have a new GM soon, and maybe a coach. And they’re holding on to a 27-year-old running back as the centerpiece of their rebuilding? Who does that?" "Taylor is a great player if he’s on a good team," an AFC scout told me. "The Colts won’t be good again for a while, which makes him dead weight. They should’ve taken the 2-plus, fixed their line, and just replaced him with someone younger." "I was shocked," the general manager told me. "Really thought he was gone. I love [Taylor], but I don’t know what they’re thinking. And I wouldn’t be shocked if the new GM tries to trade him in the offseason before free agency starts." Williams: The Chicago Bears and Jacksonville Jaguars are the biggest winners from the moves they made at this year’s trade deadline, according to league sources I spoke with. "I think Chicago and Jacksonville benefited the most," a league source told me. "They are clearly shooting their shot for a Super Bowl appearance this year." The Bears, of course, supercharged their defense with the addition of Defensive Player of the Year candidate Jeffery Simmons. Meanwhile, the Jaguars also addressed their deficiencies on defense by adding safety Jesse Bates, along with defensive tackles Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux. Chicago and Jacksonville have two of the best offenses in the league, led by Caleb Williams and Trevor Lawrence, respectively. We’ll see if the defensive upgrades push them over the edge to becoming legitimate Super Bowl contenders at the end of the year. One national scout said the Jaguars could be the biggest winners or biggest losers with their "F’ them picks" approach to trading premium picks for premium players, like the Los Angeles Rams. And that makes sense, with general manager James Gladstone and head coach Liam Coen both having spent time in Los Angeles. "The Jaguars might be the biggest winner and loser," the scout told me. "They went all in and if they win it all, then it’s a win. Or they could lose! But I like the aggressive approach because I think the race is wide open." Vacchiano: Three teams kept coming up in my discussions with league sources: The Vikings, Jaguars and the Eagles, though a few did praise the Colts and Bears, too. The Vikings praise was all about the Kirk Cousins deal. "Finding a QB who can be the difference between making the Super Bowl or not is a huge win no matter how you look at it," one NFL executive told me. "And at that price? Wow. I guarantee they would’ve given up more." The Jaguars earned praise for "going for it all," in the words of one GM. "I don’t love all their deals or what they paid," he told me, "but good for them not sitting still. There’s a reason they say ‘Fortune favors the bold’. And they were bold." The Jaguars were already loaded on offense, but added Bates, Davis and Godchaux at the deadline. "They were already a good defense," an AFC scout told me. "They made it stronger." The only question was about the price they paid for Davis, which included sending a first-round pick to the Eagles. Two sources told me that was "Way too steep." And that’s a big reason why Eagles general manager Howie Roseman was one of the winners. They had already dealt center Cam Jurgens to Baltimore for a second-round pick, and for Davis they got a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick, giving them 10 picks in the first two rounds over the next three drafts. "I’m a little surprised they didn’t do more," one general manager told me. "But they did great. They always do." The Bears, meanwhile, earned praise for acquiring Jeffrey Simmons, whom one scout told me was "the only true difference-making defensive player available." The price was high — two first-round picks. "But again," the general manager told me, "Good teams go for it. They don’t sit still." As for the Colts, despite all the questions about not trading Taylor, they did ship off guard Quenton Nelson, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and wide receivers Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, trading four players on expiring contracts for a third, two fourths, two fifths and a sixth. "Those may not seem like huge deals," one league executive told me. "But they add up. Better than letting them walk away for nothing." Williams: League sources pointed to the Indianapolis Colts as the clear losers here, giving up Quenton Nelson, Josh Downs, DeForest Buckner and Keenan Allen in a fire sale before the trade deadline. The Colts had moved on from general manager Chris Ballard, so interim general manager Ed Dodds orchestrated the moves, with the blessing of owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon. We’ll see if head coach Shane Steichen remains around at season’s end to clean up the mess. One source told me the Colts should have emptied the tank and moved on from running back Jonathan Taylor. "Indianapolis is the biggest loser by not moving Taylor and taking the reported second and fifth offered for him," the league source told me. Vacchiano: No team has taken more of a deserved beating from NFL sources around the trade deadline than the Los Angeles Chargers, who had even let teams know they were standing pat despite being 0-8 and generally a mess. They did make one deal — sending linebacker Daiyan Henley to the Broncos for a fourth- and fifth-round pick. But that was it. And then, late Wednesday night, that trade fell apart anyway. "Don’t get me started," an NFL executive told me. "Complete malpractice. They weren’t even willing to listen." "Dumbest thing I’ve seen in years," another executive told me. "I don’t know what they’re thinking. They like their players? Great. They’re doing a bang-up job for them." They almost certainly could have gotten something for players like edge rusher Khalil Mack, wide receiver Quentin Johnston and cornerback Donte Jackson, and maybe more. "But they’re sleeping," one of the NFL executives told me. "I really think nobody is home." Another loser: The Washington Commanders. But it wasn’t their fault. They had a lot of interest in defensive tackle Daron Payne, according to sources, including from the New York Giants. But Payne got hurt, ending that. "I wonder if they would’ve dealt WR Terry McLaurin before he got hurt, too," the source said. "A lot of people were looking for receivers." One other loser: The Cincinnati Bengals, "mostly for incompetence," the general manager told me. They had a deal in place with Philadelphia for depth edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie. Then a reporter on social media revealed the move would’ve meant they’d also lose a compensatory third-round pick in the next draft, and the Bengals quickly backed out of the deal. "Embarrassing," the GM told me. "How did they not know that? There are people in every organization whose job, literally, is to figure that stuff out." "I guess it’s good they found out before they lost the comp pick," an NFL executive told me. "But that’s a terrible look." It also didn’t help the Bengals’ cause that the Ebiketie deal was the only one they were apparently considering, despite a struggling defense that is holding them back. "Nobody ever accused the Bengals of being smart," one source told me.

ESPN has removed Bottomline ticker from all live games
content:
ESPN’s BottomLine survived the pager, the flip phone, and the push alert, but it will no longer survive a live sporting event on the network that created it.

According to Newsday, ESPN is removing the ticker during live action, finishing a phaseout that had already stripped the crawl from the College Football Playoff and the company’s marquee properties. Viewers watching the NFL, NBA and NHL on ESPN had grown accustomed to an unobstructed bottom third of the screen, as had audiences for tennis’s grand slams and golf’s major championships.

Asked about the expansion, an ESPN spokesperson gave Newsday the same statement, verbatim, that the network supplied to Front Office Sports in August, when college football became the first sport to lose the ticker across ESPN’s entire slate of regular-season games.

“We’re always looking for ways to better serve sports fans,” the statement read. “By removing the BottomLine during live action, we’re creating a cleaner presentation that keeps the focus where it belongs — on the field.”

That football rollout applied to every college football game on ABC, ESPN, ESPN2, SEC Network, ACC Network, ESPNU, and ESPNEWS. ESPN replaced the incessant scroll with score updates delivered at scheduled intervals each quarter, and moved programming alerts into a small graphic in the upper-right corner, where viewers learn whether a kickoff has been shifted to another channel because an earlier game ran long. Audiences for the Little League World Series saw a prototype of that graphic in late August, shortly before the football news broke.

College basketball followed when the season tipped off on Nov. 2. Viewers on the main ESPN network saw a redesigned scorebug above an empty strip where the ticker once ran, and the omission became the network’s policy for live game action going forward. To keep fans informed about games elsewhere, select broadcasts featured a graphic in the upper-right corner cycling through scores from around the sport, borrowing the solution ESPN devised for football.

ESPN still intends to keep the BottomLine alive in other corners of its programming. The ticker will continue running throughout pregame, halftime, and postgame studio coverage, and it will reappear during weather delays or whenever significant breaking news or a programming change warrants it. News and talk shows could retain the crawl, too.

For most of its existence, the BottomLine was indispensable. A fan watching Alabama in Tuscaloosa had no other way to monitor a score in Columbus without changing the channel, and ESPN built a reputation as the trusted custodian of that information. The smartphone chipped away at that arrangement, alerting viewers to every final, injury, and trade the moment it happened and turning the crawl into a belated recap of news nearly everyone watching had already seen.

Meanwhile, the ticker kept eating up space at the bottom of the screen during games, and with most of the audience following scores on a phone or tablet anyway, the case for removing it from live broadcasts only got stronger. Even so, the college football change drew a mixed response from viewers, and some fans lamented losing a dependable companion through those marathon Saturdays.

But even those fans probably had a phone within reach, with every score the ticker would have shown just a tap away.

title: Blue Jays Rumors: Valenzuela, Clement, Smith, Schneider, Pitching
content:
The hot stove is warming up. The Blue Jays haven’t made a big move yet but the buzz on them continues to be that they’re exploring just about everything. Mitch Bannon of The Athletic as well as Ben-Nicholson Smith and Shi Davidi of Sportsnet have details on some of the various things that are up in the air with the club.

Bannon notes that the Jays are getting some trade interest in catcher Brandon Valenzuela. Bannon doesn’t specify which clubs are calling but notes that the Reds have had previous interest. Valenzuela had an encouraging debut this year, getting into 91 games for the Jays. He made 271 plate appearances and hit .222/.307/.372. That translates to a 93 wRC+, indicating he was 7% worse than the league average hitter. Catchers are usually 10 to 12% below par, so that’s actually decent production, especially for a backup. Valenzuela also received strong grades for his glovework. FanGraphs credited him with 2.1 wins above replacement.

The Jays could certainly keep Valenzuela as backup to Alejandro Kirk. However, if some other club considers him to be a viable everyday catcher and is willing to pay for him accordingly in terms of a trade return, it could be worth Toronto’s while. In theory, the Jays could flip Valenzuela for a bat or an arm or a package of players and then turn to free agency to find a backup for Kirk.

Elsewhere, Bannon mentions that there’s some trade interest for infielder Ernie Clement and infielder/outfielder Davis Schneider. There are a few moving pieces in Toronto’s infield/bench situation. They have been connected to various middle infield targets already this offseason, including Brandon Lowe, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and plenty of others.

The Jays had Andrés Giménez and Clement as their primary middle infielders this year. If they add an external option, that could push Clement into a short-side platoon role with Giménez while also bouncing around to other spots. Bannon suggests that it may be difficult for both Clement and Josh Smith to hold down utility roles on the same roster. Both are multi-positional guys, Clement broadly with better defense while Smith has shown a higher offensive ceiling.

Nicholson-Smith tweets that Smith played his way into the club’s plans with his performance after being acquired from the Rangers at the deadline. Smith slashed .184/.276/.408 as a Jay but with an unlucky .200 batting average on balls in play in that small sample. The 2026 season wasn’t his best but he hit .254/.336/.380 for a 107 wRC+ with the Rangers over 2024 and 2025.

Both Smith and Clement are under club control through 2028. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects Clement for a $7.6MM salary next year and Smith $3.7MM. Clement is out of options but Smith is not. In theory, the Jays could sign a second baseman, trade Clement and then have Smith take up some of Clement’s previous duties as a utility guy. Whether the Jays go down that road or not naturally depends on the trade offers and how their free agent pursuits play out.

Schneider has shown some nice abilities at the plate, especially against lefties, but his offense is mercurial. He hit .234/.361/.436 in 2025 but just .145/.310/.315 in 2026. He is projected for a $1.3MM salary in arbitration and still has an option remaining. He has a bit of defensive versatility, eligible to move between second base and left field. The Jays are looking to upgrade both of those spots this winter. They could keep Schneider as a depth option but it makes sense to see if he has some trade value, especially if they make big additions.

Turning to the pitching staff, the Jays are looking to make upgrades there, particularly in the rotation. They have Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage and José Soriano in three spots but the options for the back end are more questionable.

Bannon mentions Freddy Peralta as a guy the Jays have interest in, though he adds that he doesn’t appear to be a high priority for them. Bannon also mentions that the Jays would be open to reunions with Kevin Gausman, Max Scherzer or Shane Bieber.

Nicholson-Smith and Davidi mention Michael Soroka and Kris Bubic as potential upside plays. Both pitchers are talented but prone to injuries. In theory, either one could provide big return on investment if he could stay healthy for a full season.

Soroka tossed 116 innings this year, his highest tally since 2019. Various injuries sidelined him in the intervening seasons. This year’s work resulted in a 3.41 earned run average, 24.1% strikeout rate and 6.1% walk rate. Bubic has a 2.98 ERA, 25.5% strikeout rate, 8.1% walk rate and 48.6% ground ball rate over the past four seasons but has only thrown 217 2/3 innings over that span because of various injuries. MLBTR predicted Soroka for a two-year, $26MM deal with an opt-out while Bubic was predicted for a one-year deal worth $12.5MM.

The Jays are one of the contenders in the Tarik Skubal bidding. It seems like Skubal plans to sign before the lockout arrives, so perhaps the Jays will wait to see how that plays out before seriously engaging other starters, but it makes sense to keep tabs on some fallback plans in case Skubal signs elsewhere.

In the bullpen, Nicholson-Smith and Davidi mention Alex Vesia as a guy the Jays have shown interest in. Vesia is considered one of the top lefties available behind Adrián Morejón. Toronto’s bullpen is in decent shape, so it’s not a huge priority. However, it would be nice to add another southpaw so they wouldn’t have to rely so heavily on Mason Fluharty, who made 83 appearances this year.

Cubs Notes: Ramirez, Kelly, Hoyer, Staffing
content:
The Cubs have two spots to fill in the outfield alongside newly minted NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong with Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki heading to free agency. The internal replacements include Pedro Ramirez, Matt Shaw, and Kevin Alcantara. Ramirez could be the leader in the clubhouse based on recent comments from GM Carter Hawkins.

The lead exec praised Ramirez’ athleticism and work ethic, factors that could help him transition into a more versatile role, as relayed by Meghan Montemurro of the Chicago Tribune. The 22-year-old primarily played second and third base in the minors, but played some first base and left field after his big-league promotion.

“There’s a risk to going with some unproven guys, but that allows you maybe to get some more proven guys in other spots,” Hawkins said. “I don’t think there’s one path that we necessarily would cross out at this juncture.”

Ramirez forced his way to the majors by hitting .312 with nine homers and 19 steals in 43 games at Triple-A. He held his own in his first taste of the highest level, slashing .261/.321/.402 across 266 plate appearances. Ramirez added six homers and nine steals. The thefts have always been a part of his profile, but the power was a big addition in 2026. He’d totaled 25 homers in four pro seasons before popping 15 this year.

Shaw got a crack as an everyday outfielder to open this past season with Suzuki dealing with an injury. He didn’t hold onto a regular job once everyone was healthy, but did manage a respectable 106 wRC+ over 202 plate appearances. Shaw has been a plus defender in minimal outfield reps. He’s also been a standout contributor with the glove at third base, though there’s no room for him there with Alex Bregman in town.

Alcantara has played in parts of three MLB seasons. That’s only amounted to 37 games, though. He’s yet to get an extended look with the Cubs and has struggled in his 50 career plate appearances. Alcantara is out of options, which might incline the club to keep him around. He has experience at all three outfield spots.

Here are a few other items from the Cubs…

  • Hawkins mentioned that bringing back free agent catcher Carson Kelly is a possibility, while adding that the team is comfortable sticking with internal options (per Montemurro). That would likely be Miguel Amaya tag-teaming the role with prospect Owen Ayers. Kelly was an above-average producer at the plate in both seasons with the Cubs. Chicago ranked 10th in OPS at the position, with the majority of that damage coming from Kelly and Amaya.
  • President of baseball operations Jed Hoyer agreed to a multi-year contract extension midway through the 2025 season. Patrick Mooney and Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic reported this week that it’s a five-year deal. Since Hoyer’s last deal was set to expire at the end of the 2025 campaign, it seems he’ll be in his role through the 2030 season. Hoyer joined the Cubs at the end of 2011. He was part of the brain trust that put together the 2016 World Series winner. Hoyer stepped into the lead role after Theo Epstein departed in 2020.
  • Mooney and Sharma also reported that Chicago hired Rylan Domingues to be a pitching analytics coordinator. Domingues has spent the past three seasons as a pitching development analyst with the Phillies. Before joining the pro ranks, he worked at training facility Tread Athletics.
  • In a separate post, Mooney reported that Ben Martin is taking over as the organization’s farm director. The duties were vacated after Jason Kanzler left to be the Mariners’ manager. Martin served as the assistant director of major league development last season. He’s held various roles in player development since being hired in 2021.

title: 4 Things Pochettino Must Fix At Manchester United
content: So there you have it. On Friday, Mauricio Pochettino shed his tears in an emotional press conference ahead of the United States men’s national team’s Concacaf Nations League two-legged quarterfinal series against Haiti, confirming what we all knew. The Argentinian is off to Manchester United with a desire to once again reclaim redemption as the 54-year-old manager – formerly at Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea — feels he has unfinished business in the Premier League. The job is clear. To help a muddled United in complete disarray, which finds itself in 18th place with eight points from the first 10 league matches. This is the club’s worst start in the top flight in 40 years, of course the arrival of a certain Alex Ferguson. What would follow would be a period of glorious dominance throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, including 2012-2013, when the club won its last Premier League trophy to date, making it a record 20 league titles. Funnily enough, that was the year when a bright-eyed and eager Argentinian entered the Premier League to take over Southampton. At the time, there were plenty of question marks over Pochettino’s introduction, notably because most of the English press knew little about the incredible work he had done with La Liga minnows Espanyol, which included an early win over Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona. But after Southampton and Tottenham Hotspur, where he guided Spurs to four consecutive top-four finishes, a Champions League final and had it not been for a miraculous Leicester City run, perhaps even a Premier League title, Pochettino earned the respect and friendship of the aforementioned Ferguson, who perhaps knew something we didn’t. This was a manager who could one day take over Man United. In fact, with Fergie three years out of management and Pochettino at Tottenham (second season where Spurs ended third), they were publicly spotted having lunch in Mayfair in London back in 2016 – thus enforcing the belief of their deep respect for each other. How could you not like Pochettino? As a person, much like his mentor Marcelo Bielsa, he is brutally honest, direct and only demands an absolute hunger for the game, no matter your title or reputation. But Pochettino has something Bielsa never mastered, which is charisma. And it’s this charisma that must collectively work with his football on the pitch to resuscitate Man United. So as Pochettino becomes the first ever South American to take over the Red Devils as head coach, I see this situation with the club very much as the football version of "Mary Poppins." First we have the Man United fanbase, playing the role of the children, Jane and Michael Banks. All they want is love, attention and someone to care for their club. The Glazer ownership, Sir Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS — acting very much like George Banks — begrudgingly have hired once again someone who can fix this mess. Enter Mary Poppins. Mauricio Pochettino. The internal and external problems are as long as Jane and Michael’s list, but the hope is for their new manager to create magic and help them climb out of this conundrum. It will, however, take more than Dick Van Dyke to save this mess, but I think Mar—I mean, Pochettino – is up to the task. Here’s what Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix immediately. It is a clear affirmation that the anger that stems from Man United is not on the head coach. It is on the ownership. We as analysts and pundits have talked about this endlessly and it’s extremely clear that there is a detached, hierarchical, strategic problem within the club. But the Glazer ownership, INEOS—they’re not going anywhere in the near future. Pochettino’s arrival, despite being a band-aid over a gunshot wound, needs to be about mending a broken relationship. I’ll get to the tactical outlook on the pitch in a moment, but the overall objective is for the Argentinian to arrive at Carrington and begin to set a precedent of trust between himself, the players, stakeholders and most importantly, the fanbase. He needs them on his side from the very first minute. The best way to do that is to speak to the press with honesty, to initiate a culture of blue-collar, hard-work effort on the training pitch, and to speak to the fans, about the fans, with the fans as much as possible. This is a Pochettino speciality. He connects with people better than most head coaches and it’s his job from day one, to place the first brick towards the bridge of trust and mutual respect. The late legendary basketball coach John Wooden would always say, "nothing will work unless you do," and I think that needs to be graffitied at the training facility in Carrington. Pochettino is known for his detailed -focused routines and gargantuan demands in training, but it all begins with accountability. He is a student of Bielsa and no one asks more of you as a person or athlete than the man whose nicknamed is "Loco." Pochettino is the same. And I think United’s number one responsibility is to heighten every asset of training. From eating habits to where you sit at lunch or how you warm up. Pochettino will demand perfection in practice, meaning that a few players will probably get a wake-up call when he arrives next Wednesday. What if I told you that the only teams in the Premier League who have conceded more goals are Ipswich Town and manager-less, bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace? United has given up 19 goals, which is just too much after 10 matches. Their defensive unit is in peril, and it’s not just about the individual, it’s a collective responsibility that lives within the midfield too. Pochettino, therefore, has to find a way to make United stronger at the back, beginning with a daunting trip to Anfield a week on Sunday. This isn’t a Pochettino strength per se, as his focus is high pressure and fluidity in the final third. But this has to be a major task for the Argentinian. As I mentioned before, the mental issues with United are obvious, and it’s important to instill belief into the squad. I think about 21-year-old defender Lenny Yoro, for example, who desperately needs guidance. Or the obvious one, Kobbie Mainoo. He is such a talented midfielder, but what he has needed most is a proverbial arm around his shoulder. Pochettino has a fantastic history of developing and nurturing young players. England striker Harry Kane – who became a Tottnham legend under Pochettino's guidance – has alluded to this. Cavan Sullivan, the teenage U.S. star, constantly speaks about Pochettino’s belief in the young Philadelphia Union attacker. Younger members of United, therefore, need Pochettino more than ever. But I also think the veterans need it too, beginning of course with midfielder Bruno Fernandes and centerback Harry Maguire. It’s imperative for Pochettino to replace doubt with strength, and finger-pointing with accountability. I believe Pochettino can help this squad because this isn’t the same manager who left Chelsea in 2024. The Argentinian found a new version of himself with the U.S. and I’d like to think he arrives at Man United, not as a savior, but a warrior, who can help these down-and-out players pick themselves up again. Or, in retrospect, as Mary Poppins flying down from the skies with a magical umbrella, ready to save — not London — but the west side of Manchester.

title: Boomer Esiason and Gregg Giannotti lose it after burp, sniffing glue smells
content:
Boomer Esiason and Gregg Giannotti took the phrase “feel good Friday” to a new level on their WFAN morning show.

Audacy’s New York studios where WFAN is located has been under construction for months. And it’s created some challenges for the hosts, with added noise, closed bathrooms and coffee stations. But surely, no one expected to get high off the construction.

WFAN recently moved into its new studio which features digital screens and no décor. But with work continuing in the building, the smell of glue permeated the studio Friday morning while Esiason and Giannotti were on-air.

“We’re sniffing straight up glue right now,” Giannotti said. “We are sucking in with every breath, severe glue stank. Every sniff. Right into the lungs.”

Audacy spent a lot of money to renovate its New York studios and it’s largely been criticized by WFAN hosts as they navigated months of construction. Even listeners have been disappointed with the new studio trading décor and memorabilia for a digital screen. But the construction finally led to some good vibes Friday morning.

The glue stank was so strong that Giannotti and Esiason insisted they were getting high off it, and they proved it with an uncontrollable fit of laughter that erupted over a hot mic burp.

Gio completely broke Boomer with a hot mic burp https://t.co/tRkPidj15w

— WFAN Sports Radio (@WFAN660) November 13, 2026

“This is gonna be one of those days we talk about for years, remember the day we got high off the glue from the construction?” Giannotti said through continued laughter.

Eventually, someone went to the area of construction and found they were painting the walls with glue, likely a noise proofing compound, and urged the workers to open windows because the smell was traveling through air vents into the WFAN studio. The open windows solved the issue, until Boomer and Gio finished the show feeling like they were hungover from the high.

Chris Russo often talks about his love for weed gummies, teasing the possibility of eating one before his radio show or an episode of First Take. Boomer and Gio inadvertently proved the on-air high can be fun for a bit, until that high starts to wear off.

Second-Half Breakout Candidates: 25 Players Who Could Emerge In Season's Homestretch
content: We already know which players have been the best of the best so far in this NFL season. In fact, a few of my colleagues ranked the top 50 players so far this season earlier this week. But there are many other players who might not be on your radar that are in a position to break out in the second half of the season. So, we are digging into players who, for one reason or another, could break out and surprise you the rest of the way. Some of these players have missed time with injury. Others were buried on the depth chart, but will now see extra playing time following Tuesday's trade deadline. And we also have players who had solid showings in the first half of the year and might be in line to have a bigger role in the second half of the season. Then, there are the rookies who are starting to get more playing time, like Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza, who is in a prime spot to break out. So, let's take a look at which lesser-known players can make a name for themselves over the next couple of months. Can a No. 1 overall pick be a sleeper? We'll allow it, if only because he had been relegated to the bench for the first half of 2026, with one eight-pass cameo in a lopsided loss to the Patriots as his only game action. And with the Raiders trading Kirk Cousins this week, Mendoza now has a runway to spark some excitement in Las Vegas ahead of the 2027 season. Branch missed the first five games recovering from a torn Achilles tendon, but his healthy return will be a spark for the Lions defense, which gave up 73 points in two losses without him. Detroit is 4-2 and can absolutely contend for the NFC North title with a healthy secondary. Branch had seven interceptions in his first two years with the Lions, including a Pro Bowl nod in 2024. Even at 3-5, New Orleans isn't out of contention in the NFC South, and the Saints just welcomed back Tyson, the No. 8 overall pick in this year's draft. His hamstring injury kept him away for the first seven games of the season, but the Saints needed a talented complement to Chris Olave. He only had four catches for 30 yards in his debut last week. However, Tyson had 18 touchdowns in his last two seasons at Arizona State. Tyler Shough has 13 touchdown passes without him to start the year. Denver is 7-2 but ranks 29th in total offense and 27th in rushing, so the healthy return of Coleman from an ankle injury could really help. He's gotten an increase in touches over the last two weeks, logging 21 touches last week against the Panthers. The fourth-round rookie from Washington has more upside than either J.K. Dobbins (3.3 yards per carry) or RJ Harvey (3.6 yards per carry). As Denver chases the Chiefs, a consistent run game would help Bo Nix immensely. The Jets have a lot invested in Breece Hall, but Allen ran well stepping in while New York's lead back was injured. He rushed for 565 yards in the first eight games, more than he totaled in his first two seasons with the Jets. He's still only 22, and making a case for a much larger role in the offense. That wasn't on display in Hall's return, when Allen only had eight carries in a loss to the Chiefs. But has Allen topped 100 yards twice in three weeks, something Hall has never done in his NFL career. Trading DeForest Buckner to the 49ers was a huge loss for the Colts, but Adebawore's emergence helps offset it, as seen in a two-sack game in their loss to the Vikings. The 2023 fourth-rounder from Northwestern had four sacks last year and has already matched that in 2026. His increased playing time with Buckner gone could set him up for a payday as a 2027 free agent. Colts would be wise to lock him up. Ponder is already a success story, making New England's roster last year as an undrafted rookie out of Cal Poly. He had four sacks last year and already has 7.5 in 2026, with a forced fumble and a fumble-return touchdown. Undrafted players are eligible for extensions after only two seasons, and if Ponder continues his play, New England could sign him to a long-term deal before he gets expensive. San Francisco has won despite a huge rash of injuries at receiver, and Stribling has been sidelined since he sprained his ankle in the season opener. The 33rd overall pick this year out of Ole Miss had rave reviews in preseason, and if the 49ers are to make any kind of push in the playoffs, they'll need a talented complement to Mike Evans. They got Keenan Allen at the trade deadline, but the 49ers probably need a little youth in that receiver room, too. Former first-rounder Ashton Jeanty has struggled to consistently gain yards running the ball. He's averaged 3.2 yards per carry, while Washington has averaged 3.9 as a fourth-round rookie out of New Mexico State. As the Raiders have shifted to a rookie quarterback, this rookie could continue to chip into Jeanty's role if he can produce consistently. Seattle has missed Kenneth Walker, and the injury to Price, their first-round pick out of Notre Dame, has been a big part of that. Seattle ranks 25th in yards per carry, and Price had 119 yards in his first three games before he was sidelined with a chest injury. Having him and Zach Charbonnet back healthy will help the Seahawks as they try to challenge the 49ers for the NFC West title and a playoff push. Offensive injuries have scuttled the Eagles' season, but Lemon has been a rare bright spot, getting his first touchdown catch as part of a seven-catch, 67-yard breakout game against Dallas in Week 7. He's logged 57 and 61 yards, respectively, over the Eagles' last two games. With DeVonta Smith hurt, this first-round rookie is challenging for the team lead in receptions, and finding success despite having backup quarterbacks throwing to him with Jalen Hurts out with his blood clot issues. Much like Brian Branch, Joseph has been sorely missed in Detroit. He's nearing a return from his knee injury, and is now the NFL's highest-paid safety after totaling 20 interceptions in his first four NFL seasons. The Lions have only six takeaways in six games, and if they're going to keep up in the toughest division in the NFL, they need their best playmakers healthy and leading that charge. Cooper hurt his ankle after only one catch in the season opener, but came back with a fury, topping 100 yards in games against the Patriots and Dolphins with a touchdown in both games. The Jets are 2-7 but are set up with three high first-round picks, and whichever rookie is at quarterback in 2027, Cooper should be a key part of an emerging offense for New York next season. The fourth-round rookie from Miami is the Bucs' nickel defensive back, fourth on the team in tackles as a part-time player. He's adept as a blitzer and will get more chances that way, but he's also active on special teams, with four tackles there in Tampa Bay's rout of the Panthers. He's a versatile piece who will get more involved at the line of scrimmage when Antoine Winfield returns healthy at safety. Mahogany struggled in 11 starts last year but has been a pleasant surprise at left guard, especially for a 2024 sixth-round pick out of Boston College. Getting center Cade Mays healthy gives them a surplus of starter-caliber linemen on the interior, but he should hold onto his spot next to All-Pro tackle Penei Sewell. Pro Football Focus rates him as the NFL's 10th-best guard this season. Jacksonville let Travis Etienne leave in free agency, trusting that Tuten could step in as the primary running back, and he's rushed for 521 yards and four touchdowns in the Jaguars' first eight games. He's been consistent, going for at least 60 yards in each of his first five games, and will get a larger workload with two games each left against the lowly Titans and Colts, who just dealt away star DTs. How would you like to take over for Quenton Nelson? That's likely the opportunity ahead for Farmer, a fourth-round rookie out of Kentucky who didn't play a single offensive snap before the Nelson trade. Indy's fire sale means there isn't much to play for beyond evaluating the existing talent, so it's his best chance to show they don't need to draft a guard with all those new draft picks. The third-round rookie from Notre Dame had his second touchdown in the Patriots' loss to the Bears and had 52 receiving yards this past week against the Packers. While Hunter Henry is second on New England in receiving yards, Raridon should see his role increase in the second half of the season. He's already matched the two touchdowns Austin Hooper had as TE2 last season, and Drake Maye spreads the ball around in a deep passing game. Daniels had the clinching interception in the 49ers' home win over the undefeated 49ers, and he and fellow rookie linebacker Harold Perkins have played a ton in the middle of the Falcons' defense. He's started every game and leads all Atlanta linebackers in tackles, a solid impact for the fourth-round pick from Oklahoma. Ojomo could have been traded at the deadline, but Philadelphia traded Jordan Davis to Jacksonville instead, suggesting that the Eagle will be willing to write a big check to keep Ojomo from free agency. The 2023 seventh-rounder had six sacks last year and will play much more with Davis gone. He's from the Milton Williams school of promising third-string defensive tackles who get massive contracts, likely $20 million a year or more. There isn't much to see with the Eagles, but watch him. The Eagles have been decimated by injuries on offense, and that includes their second-round pick from Vanderbilt, who is in position to take the reins from Dallas Goedert in a long run of prolific Eagles tight ends. Philadelphia brought Zach Ertz in as emergency depth, but Stowers, a converted quarterback, has a chance to step up as a solid TE2, eventually taking the top spot from Goedert. Only one rookie in the last 10 years has had more than five interceptions (Seattle's Tariq Woolen had six in 2022), but Masses has three in the Raiders' first nine games. The fifth-round pick from Cal contributed to Las Vegas' unexpected 3-0 start, though the more the Raiders are trailing, the less opponents will have reason to throw as much. Jacksonville has a top-10 scoring offense, and the Jaguars have done so with Pregnon taking every snap of every game at left guard. The Jaguars have pushed through injuries at tackle, but are set up for a second-half surge as they did last year with easy opponents. They've gotten contributions from other rookies on offense in receiver Josh Cameron and tight end Nate Boerkircher. The Chargers didn't trade Khalil Mack at the deadline, but Los Angeles would be wise to give its first-round rookie some more snaps. He has 2.5 sacks in the first eight games coming off the bench. He put up better initial production than fellow Miami first-rounder Rueben Bain, who has one sack so far with the Bucs. He goes from a Miami Hurricanes team that lost three games to a Chargers team that might not win three this year. Somebody has to catch passes with Josh Downs and Keenan Allen traded away at the deadline. Gould will have a chance to step in as the slot receiver. He's tiny at 5-foot-8, 174 pounds, a 2024 fifth-round pick from Oregon State who has totaled four catches for 45 yards in 25 games over three seasons. Ashton Dulin (44 catches in seven seasons) will get more targets, but watch for Gould, who ran a 4.39 at the combine and had 718 receiving yards as a college senior in 2023.

Cubs, White Sox, Padres Among Teams Interested In Kaima Taira
content:
Right-hander Kaima Taira, star for the Seibu Lions of Japan’s Nippon Professional Baseball, is drawing widespread interest after being posted for major league clubs. Bruce Levine of 670 The Score in Chicago reports that both the Cubs and White Sox have “strong” interest in Taira. They were both planning to meet with agent Scott Boras this week, though the Boras Corporation of course represents a large number of this winter’s free agents beyond just Taira. Kevin Acee of the San Diego Union-Tribune writes that while the Padres have some level of interest in all three NPB stars who were posted this winter — slugger Teruaki Sato and righty Hiromi Itoh being the others — the Friars seem particularly focused on Taira.

The Blue Jays were known to have scouted Taira extensively this past season and have carried their interest into the offseason, per Sportsnet’s Shi Davidi. Toronto has done “lots of background work” on Taira, per the report. Davidi adds that Taira isn’t traveling to North America to meet with interested clubs in person but is conducting frequent Zoom calls with teams major league clubs. That presumably includes Toronto, though it’s not clear whether the two parties have formally spoken or are still lining up a time to do so. The Giants also have some interest in Taira and have discussed him internally, according to John Shea of the San Francisco Standard.

That early list of teams is surely just a sampling of clubs who have interest in signing the 26-year-old Taira (27 this weekend). The right-hander was scouted by upwards of half the teams in Major League Baseball throughout the 2026 season as he posted dominant results out of the Lions’ rotation in Japan. The Mets, Angels, Rangers, Yankees and Mariners are all known to have scouted Taira this past season as well, though the latter two teams are quite deep in rotation arms and aren’t necessarily likely to jump into Taira’s market.

Taira is an oddity in every sense of the word. Listed at just 5’8″ and 209 pounds, he’s built like Alejandro Kirk but sits 95-97 mph on his four seamer and can ramp the pitch up into the triple digits. He just posted a 1.36 ERA, 24.8% strikeout rate, 7.9% walk rate and 48.5% ground-ball rate in 146 innings this past season in Japan. Scouts who spoke to MLBTR about Taira have indicated that he holds his velocity deep into starts and will often work on the low end of his velo early in games before ramping up in the late innings when he’s ready to empty the proverbial tank.

The numbers and velocity scream “future big league starter,” but Taira’s body type is almost unheard of for a major league pitcher. Marcus Stroman is the closest recent example — a 5’8″, 170-pound righty of whom many teams were skeptical as a starter early in his professional career. Stroman is an anomaly, however. Few players of this height and build have even pitched in the majors, let alone held up through the rigors of a starting pitcher’s workload.

Some teams will surely hope to deploy Taira as a reliever. He’s worked out of the bullpen in all but two of his NPB seasons. The Lions moved him to the rotation in 2023 and found great success (2.40 ERA in 150 frames), but he suffered an injury after five starts in 2024, missed several months, and returned as a reliever. He was back in the ‘pen come 2025, but the Lions again stretched him out to great effect in 2026. The evaluators who spoke to MLBTR about Taira over the past month suggested that even though some teams will hope to plug him into the ‘pen, he’s extremely likely to prioritize signing as a starting pitcher.

Either Chicago team makes good sense as a landing spot. The Cubs are no strangers to signing Japanese stars (e.g. Seiya Suzuki, Shota Imanaga, Kosuke Fukudome) and saw an entire rotation’s worth of arms reach free agency at season’s end. They’ll be without Cade Horton early next year as he recovers from April UCL surgery, and they received nothing from Justin Steele in 2026 following his own UCL procedure early in the 2025 campaign, as he experienced setbacks along the way. Righty Ben Brown recently underwent spinal surgery as well, further limiting the Cubs’ supply of starters.

The White Sox, meanwhile, have already declared adding to the rotation their top priority. GM Chris Getz revealed that powerhouse reliever Grant Taylor will move into the rotation in 2027, and the South Siders have a smattering of interesting mid-rotation arms: Sean Burke, Noah Schultz, Davis Martin and Anthony Kay among them. It seems likely they’ll add at least one established major league starter to the fray, but they have more than enough payroll space to make two prominent rotation additions. The Sox haven’t been big players in the market for NPB stars in the past but broke that trend last year with their surprise signing of slugger Munetaka Murakami.

As for the Padres, they touch base on virtually every star player who becomes available, whether that’s an established big leaguer or a high-end player from NPB or the Korea Baseball Organization. Taira is no exception, but it’s of note that Acee suggests Taira is the focus over Sato and Itoh. The Friars have a skeleton crew in the rotation right now, with Joe Musgrove standing as the only starting pitcher on their staff who’s previously worked a full, successful season in a big league rotation. Musgrove, however, missed all of the 2025-26 seasons due to injury and only returned to the mound during the 2026 postseason. There’s no telling what to expect from him next year.

San Diego also has Randy Vasquez, JP Sears, Jhony Brito and newly signed Ryan Weiss in the running for innings. It’s possible Yu Darvish will be back after missing the 2026 season, but he’s now 40 years old and has mulled retirement. The Padres are losing Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Casey Mize and Robbie Ray to the open market. They badly need to bring in some innings. It’s already known that they’d like to re-sign King and Pivetta, in particular, but Taira adds another interesting name to the team’s list of potential targets.

The Giants, similarly, need several arms. Adrian Houser is their nominal third starter behind Logan Webb and Landen Roupp. They lost four young pitchers — Carson Whisenhunt, Trevor McDonald, Hayden Birdsong, Blade Tidwell — to Tommy John surgery during the 2026 season. It’ll be a surprise if they don’t add at least two new rotation arms this winter.

Taira’s posting window opened on Nov. 1. Since the looming MLB lockout won’t pause the negotiation window for stars who’ve been posted by their NPB, KBO and CPBL teams, Taira is a lock to sign before the current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59pm ET on Dec. 1. In addition to whatever guarantee he and Boras negotiate, Taira’s new team will also owe a posting fee to the Lions. That sum, which is in addition to his guarantee, is equal to 20% of the contract’s first $25MM, plus 17.5% of the next $25MM and 15% of any guaranteed money thereafter. Future earnings under the contract, whether via incentives or options, are also subject to the posting fee system once that money become guaranteed.

title: Emmanuel Acho apologizes to Steph Curry over Ayesha Curry controversy
content:
Emmanuel Acho has heard Steph Curry’s criticism and apologized for his comments about his wife, Ayesha Curry.

The controversy started when Acho and other sports podcasters were up in arms over Ayesha Curry starring in a Roku Channel romcom entitled Second Chance Holiday. But what should have been a proud moment for the Curry family was derailed by bizarre criticism from the likes of LeSean McCoy, Emmanuel Acho, Gilbert Arenas, and Nick Young.

The former athletes were incredulous that Steph Curry’s wife kissed another man on screen, even though it’s called acting. While Ayesha largely laughed off the ignorant critiques, the Golden State Warriors star fiercely defended his wife and called out the podcasters by name for their misogyny.

“But this one in particular, when you’re trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife and, obviously, leading podcasts tapings and topics and giving opinions on somebody else’s wife, Nick, Gil, Emmanuel, and anybody else who feels the need to jump in and give an opinion on something you don’t really know about, something that kind of speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they’re allowed to do and what they’re not allowed to do, even the ignorance behind how acting works, obviously, I tried to laugh this one off. But something needs to be said,” Steph Curry said.

After Steph Curry’s statement, at least one of the people he mentioned has issued a formal apology.

On his Speakeasy show, Emmanuel Acho stepped up to say that he was sorry.

I’m sorry, @StephenCurry30, not “my bad” not, “that’s on me.”

I’m sorry. https://t.co/QOf1xneFTp

— Emmanuel Acho (@EmmanuelAcho) November 12, 2026

“If a man humbly comes to you and requests an apology, then you would be ignorant and you would be arrogant to respond with anything else than ‘I’m sorry.’ Steph, I’m sorry, not just for offending you, potentially offending your wife, I’m sorry for how that may have made you feel seeing headlines, commentary, all these other things about your wife,” Acho said.

“I’m sorry for the reaction that it may have caused internally, viscerally, amongst you, the central nervous system, how it set that off. I’m also sorry for any tiff or rift that it may have caused behind the scenes. I am sorry for that. Not ‘my bad,’ not ‘that’s on me,’ not ‘hey, you know what I mean.’ No, none of that. I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”

You can commend Emmanuel Acho for offering an unequivocal apology. However, it is weird that it was more directed toward Steph Curry, with a man-to-man vibe, instead of Ayesha Curry, especially given Steph took offense at the podcasters and their overall views on women. If there’s anyone who should receive an apology, isn’t it her instead of him? We’ll see if any of the others follow suit and step up to make amends with the Currys in the days ahead.

Tigers Interested In Shota Imanaga
content:
The Tigers entered the offseason in search of help in the rotation and the bullpen. They’ve already addressed the latter, adding former Reds closer Emilio Pagan this week. As far as starting pitching, Jon Morosi of MLB Network reports that left-hander Shota Imanaga is among the free agents the club is interested in.

Imanaga hit free agency last winter but ultimately stayed with the Cubs after accepting the qualifying offer. The 33-year-old is back on the market this offseason and won’t have the QO attached to him this time around. Imanaga put together 32 starts of a 3.77 ERA with nearly a strikeout per inning in 2026. He tossed a career-high 174 1/3 innings as basically the only Cubs starter to stay healthy all year.

Homers are the big issue for Imanaga. He’s a flyball pitcher with middling strikeout stuff. When the wind was blowing in at Wrigley Field, he was an elite starter. When it was blowing out, the long balls came in bunches. Only Phillies righty Aaron Nola (37) gave up more home runs than Imanaga (35) in 2026.

Comerica Park would be an upgrade for Imanaga. Statcast’s Park Factors ranked it 14th for home runs over the past three seasons. Wrigley Field comes in at No. 8 on the leaderboard. For right-handed power, there was basically no difference. Chicago ranked 11th and Detroit ranked 12th for righty homers.

Detroit moved Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize at the trade deadline. Veterans Justin Verlander (retired) and Jack Flaherty (free agent) have departed. That leaves a youthful group beyond veteran Framber Valdez. Jackson Jobe and Troy Melton are locks for rotation spots. Keider Montero and River Ryan could round out the group, with Drew Anderson potentially factoring in. Reese Olson is working his way back from shoulder surgery. It’s an intriguing unit, but far from rock solid, which could lead to additions.

“We’re just trying to build the deepest list we can,” president of baseball operations Scott Harris told reporters, including Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic. “If there’s opportunity to add multiple (starters), like one via trade and one via free agency, we’re definitely going to explore that.”

Imanaga came in at No. 21 on our Top 50 Free Agents list. We predicted a two-year, $40MM deal for him. Detroit closed the season with a payroll of $202,140,280, per our Payroll Tracker. That figure is down to $149,175,536 right now. There should be some flexibility to spend if the club plans on getting back closer to the $200K range. The Tigers have minimal long-term commitments outside of Valdez.

title: Kirk Herbstreit dumps on Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’
content:
Amazon was probably eager to have Thursday Night Football promote its massive commitment to Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, until Kirk Herbstreit chimed in.

With the third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power premiering this week, Al Michaels had a read to promote the series while coming out of a commercial break during the third quarter of the Washington Commanders’ 24-21 win over the New York Giants Thursday night.

Al Michaels: “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power now streaming only on Prime Video”

Kirk Herbstreit: “You know, I’ve never been a big sci-fi guy” https://t.co/Nvc1Z19Q5T

— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) November 13, 2026

“One ring to rule them all,” Michaels said before making sure Herbstreit was listening to the promo. “The epic saga returns, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, now streaming only on Prime Video.”

“You know,” Herbstreit interjected. “I’ve never been a big sci-fi guy.”

Amazon has spent over $1 billion to get Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power on Prime Video, with season 3 likely costing upwards $500 million alone, all for its Thursday Night Football debut to be met with the announcement that Herbstreit does not like sci-fi movies.

Nothing wrong with Kirk Herbstreit not being a fan of sci-fi movies or a fan of The Lord of the Rings. But what does one have to do with the other? That’s like Herbstreit hearing a promo for Harry Potter and saying, “I’ve never been a big non-fiction guy.” But in the name of being a good employee, Herbstreit will try to watch the new season.

“You just told me to dial in, so I’ll give it a shot,” Herbstreit told Michaels in an attempt to lessen the blow.

“Otherwise, our bosses will be giving us a shot,” Michaels joked in response. “And not of Ketel One either.”

Obviously, Amazon would have preferred if Herbstreit came out as a Lord of the Rings expert instead of revealing he doesn’t know what sci-fi is. But being shot over it seems a bit extreme. And in an effort to avoid being shot by their Prime Video bosses, Herbstreit will try to learn why The Lord of the Rings is not of the sci-fi genre.

title: Michael Phelps pays emotional tribute to Dan Hicks after sudden death: ‘This one hurts’
content:
On Thursday morning, Rich Lerner broke the devastating news that Dan Hicks has died. According to his wife, longtime ESPN broadcaster Hannah Storm, Hicks passed suddenly and unexpectedly “following an acute illness.” The venerated NBC Sports broadcaster was 64 years old.

Within minutes of the news, grieving colleagues and fans tried to make sense of the impossible by memorializing Hicks as the giant he was. Hicks’s unmistakable voice soundtracked countless iconic sports moments, like Tiger Woods’s Torrey Pines triumph and Michael Phelps’s Olympic glory in 2008, as Awful Announcing’s very own Matt Yoder chronicled here.

But to Phelps, Hicks wasn’t just a voice; he was a friend. And as the all-time great swimmer wrote on Instagram, he can’t believe he’s gone.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Michael Phelps (@m_phelps00)

“Man…. This one hurts,” Phelps captioned an Instagram carousel. “Really don’t even know what to say right now. There are certain voices in sports that you hear and instantly know who it is…. Dan had one of those voices. A voice that so many of us grew up listening to, a voice that brought some of the biggest moments in sports to life…. And for me, a voice that will forever be part of my story. But he was so much more than that to me. He was a friend.”

“We shared so many memories over the years, both in and out of the pool. The laughs, the conversations, the moments I’ll never forget,” Phelps continued. “Dan, thank you for the friendship, the memories, and everything you did for me and our sport. Gonna miss you, my friend. Sending all my love to Hannah and the girls [red heart emoji].”

Phelps also spoke with Karen Crouse of Sport & State and said he learned of Hicks’s passing after waking up to a text from NBC’s Mike Tirico, urging him to call immediately.

“I was in shock,” Phelps told Crouse, adding, “I grew up with him. And I got super close to Hannah, just with conversations we’ve had, whether it’s about mental health or whatever.”

Phelps additionally lamented that he won’t have the chance to share the broadcast booth with Hicks and Rowdy Gaines at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, as he’d “looked forward” to the trio “getting back together.”

The booth at the PGA Tour, Olympics, and Notre Dame football games will feel emptier now without Hicks, but Jason Benetti will do his best to honor Hicks as the replacement play-by-play announcer alongside Jason Garrett for Notre Dame-Boston College on Saturday.

title: Dan Wetzel blames CFP expansion on unpopularity of rankings show: ‘Killed the credibility of the committee’
content:
As more information comes out about the expansion of the College Football Playoff to 24 teams, one thing is certain: Almost nobody wanted this.

Just this week, The Athletic reported that even ESPN, which has broadcast rights to the entire tournament, didn’t support the idea. And a Nielsen survey showed that 90 percent of respondents who considered themselves college football fans also didn’t support it—which CFP executive director Rich Clark acknowledged (and ignored) this week.

Yet here we are, with the first 24-team bracket set to arrive next winter. And ESPN’s Dan Wetzel believes that by chasing “credibility” with the weekly rankings show, the committee dug a grave for its own credibility and forced itself to expand to please critics.

“One of the reasons we expanded this Playoff is by doing these weekly rankings over the years. They absolutely killed the credibility of the committee,” Wetzel said Wednesday on The College GameDay Podcast.

“And so every week, these things come out, it’s literally a half-baked pie, and then you let everybody tee off on you. And so it is either, in the media, people who are going to get far more engagement on the outrage algorithm of saying, ‘This is the dumbest committee of all time,’ they did this, or they did that. Or, these coaches who sit around and complain about, ‘We’re just not getting respect because we’re not this or we’re not that.'”

By opening up its deliberations to scrutiny, the committee ultimately may have revealed its own shortcomings. Beyond the complaints that Wetzel highlights, even genuine analysis of the rankings each week would underscore faulty arguments. The week-to-week selection of teams that qualify for the postseason is far less exact than a big, fancy rankings show makes it out to be.

And Wetzel believes that the committee was so sensitive to the criticism it faced that it inevitably embraced arguments from teams and conferences that used these inexact rankings cases to argue that, in fact, more teams were worthy of a Playoff berth.

“There’s an entire economy on ripping the hell out of the committee, which undermines the value of the committee and undermines that this Playoff isn’t successful, and hence we need to expand the Playoff,” Wetzel explained.

“It was not an organized activity. It was actually a self-own by the Playoff people who wanted this to work. But you can draw a pretty quick line between deciding we’re going to put out a half-baked ranking and why we went from a four-team Playoff to a 24-team Playoff in four short years. And part of it is they just allowed this to be smashed up, and it’s like, who the hell cares where they’re ranked right now? We’ll find out.”

The committee doesn’t seem to agree. The rankings will continue even under the 24-team format, though host Rece Davis acknowledged they need to be “reimagined” so as not to bore the audience with a long list of mediocre teams in the lower seeds.

But in its quest to spark conversation and be “accountable” in its process, the CFP may have put itself in a doom spiral that led to a result nobody truly asked for.
